30.       Another point brought before the Committee by the Federation of Indian Airlines is that the exorbitant cost of
 the ATF.  The Indian carriers are subject to surcharges, states sales taxation, airport throughput charges etc.   All these
 various different elements add up to the differential of 70 to 90%in excess of what fuel costs elsewhere.   Airports have
 a considerable scope to exercise market power in negotiating terms and conditions for the provisions of refueling
 services by the Oil Companies and the scope for airlines to use alternative suppliers or refuel offside is not available.  
 Therefore, they propose that fuel supply infrastructure at airports should come under the purview of AERA.  This is in
 line with the recommendations of the Naresh Chandra Committee. 
31.       In view of the submissions made by the FIA, the Committee strongly recommends that the fuel supply
 infrastructure should be brought under the purview of AERA Bill and this should be added in the powers and functions
 of the authority in Chapter 3 of the Bill.
32.       To a specific query regarding the expansion of AERA’s role and functions to cover all airports used for the
 operation of commercial flights irrespective of size of the airport or ownership, the Ministry of Civil Aviation has
 replied that 11 major airports generate/handle almost 85% of the revenue and passenger traffic.  Therefore, the scope of
 AERA is sufficiently wide.  Further the Ministry has stated that economic regulation of smaller airports would be
 cumbersome without commensurate benefits.  In any case depending on the need, the Central Government can notify
 other airports also, i.e. even those airports which have throughput less than 1.5 million passengers per annum as major
 airports.
33.       The Bill limits the powers of the authority only to major airports which are having a throughput of 1.5 million
 passengers per annum.  Jet Airways submitted that all airports are inevitable monopolies irrespective of ownership and
 the passenger throughput.  Therefore, it is necessary that the charges levied at all the airports should be subject to the
 regulation of AERA.  This will ensure that the tariffs payable at these airports are determined on the basis of some
 principles as are being laid down under the Bill and they also bear some relationship to the charges levied at major
 airports as defined in the Bill. 
34.       The Committee observes that the Airports Authority of India, did not have any fixed performance standards to
 serve the passengers or to that matter for the efficiency of the airports.  The Bill presently covers only major airports
 handling 1.5 million or more passengers per annum.  The Committee does not find any reason to exclude about 116 odd
 other airports from the purview of the present Bill.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the role of AERA and
 its functions should be expanded to cover all the airports used for the operation of commercial flights irrespective of the
 size of the airport or ownership or throughput of passengers. 
35.       The Authority will also determine the amount of development fees in respect of major airports as per Clause 13
 (1) (b).   Development fees are a new syndrome which is being introduced in the Indian aviation sector. 
 Commissioning of new Greenfield private airports at Hyderabad and Bangalore has paved the way for introduction of
 user development fees on the passengers for using the airports.   Pending the AERA set-up, both the operators at these
 Greenfield airports have already fixed different rate of development fees for the passengers.
36.       The main question before the regulator will be quantum of development fees which will be charged on the
 passengers.  Since this will be a new phenomenon in the Indian aviation sector, response from the passengers will be a
 varied one.  Any amount of development fees will definitely increase the cost of air travel which will finally have an
 impact on the viability of the airlines.
37.       The Committee hopes that any amount of development fee which will be fixed by the AERA should not dampen
 the passenger demand.  The Committee is of the opinion that making air travel expensive by such development fees
 will have a significant impact on the overall economy, especially, on the tourism, commerce and hospitality sectors. 
 The Committee hopes that the proposed regulator will definitely play a positive and critical role in determining
 development fees.

69.       This Clause relates to the amendment of the Aircraft Act, 1934 and the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994.
 The proposed amendments are of consequential nature and amendments shall take effect on the date of establishment of
 the Authority.
70.       Clause 55 reads - "  (1) If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of this Act, the Central
 Government may, by order published in the Official   Gazette, make such provisions, not inconsistent with the
 provisions of this Act, as             may appear to it to be necessary for removing the difficulty:
Provided that no order shall be made under this section after the expiry of          two years from the date of
 commencement of this Act.
(2) Every order made under this section shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is          made, before each House
 of Parliament".
71.       This Clause relates to the power of the Central Government to remove difficulties. This Clause confers power
 upon the Central Government to make, by order, published in the Official Gazette, such provisions, not inconsistent
 with the provisions of this proposed legislation, as may appear to it to be necessary for removing the difficulty, if any,
 which arises in giving effect to the provisions of this proposed legislation. However, no such order shall be made under
 this Clause after the expiry of two years from the date of commencement of this proposed legislation. This Clause
 further requires that every order made under this Clause shall be laid before each House of Parliament.

72.       When the Committee raised some queries over the sweeping powers of the Authority vide Clauses 43-48 like no
 suit, prosecution or other legal proceedings shall lie against the Central Government or the Authority or any member,
 officer or other employees thereof for anything which is done in good faith and also the non-taxation of profits of the
 Authority, the Secretary responded that the Central Government can supersede the Authority as mentioned in the
 Clause 49 of the Bill.
73.       The Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice while responding to the abovementioned queries has
 stated that the provisions of Clause 43 has incorporated this policy to strengthen the legal status of the Chairperson,
 Members and the officials or the Authority so that they may effectively discharge their duties envisaged under the law. 
 As for as Clause 44 is concerned, they have stated that whenever an Authority is created under the law to determine the
 tariff in respect of a service, no other forum should determine the same matter for the purpose of certainty and
 avoidance of multiplicity of conflict on jurisdiction on the issues involved.   This Clause is also necessary for the
 purpose to avoid parallel proceedings at two places in respect of the same matter.
74.       The Legislative Department has also stated that the provisions of Clause 45 aim to provide protection in respect
 of action taken in good faith.  It has been the policy of law not to protect the actions which are in bad faith, actuated by
 malice, ill-will or deliberate misuse of powers, as it has been the golden thread of the rule of law.  However, the honest
 and bonafide actions must be protected by the law for the efficient discharge of duties by the officials.  The provisions
 of Clause 45 are necessary in a legislation creating an authority for the purpose of effective functioning of the Members
 and Officials of the Authority.  The Indian Penal Code has also provided general exception to the offence in respect of
 actions and omissions done in good faith.  Therefore, it has been consistent legal policy to uphold protection in law for
 the acts and omissions done in good faith.
75.       Regarding Clause 47 the Department has further stated the Chapter VI of the proposed legislation contains
 offences and penalties under sections 37 to 41.  Sections 37 to 39 provide for the punishment of non-compliance of the
 orders of the Authority and the Appellate Authority and of the orders and directions given under this Act.  Sections 40
 and 41 provide for the punishment of the officers in case the offences committed by the companies and the Government
 Departments.  Hence, it is necessary that no prosecution may be initiated in respect of the offences under this Act
 except on an authorization by the Authority so that the Authority may effectively monitor the performance standard at
 the airports.
76.       When the Committee enquired about  the delegation of powers of the Authority as mentioned in Clause 48 of the
 Bill, the Legislative Department replied that there is a Chairperson and Members in the Authority and decision of the
 Authority is arrived by the collective participation and discussion of views of all the Members and the chairperson in
 the Authority.  It may not be always convenient to call for the meeting of the Authority where all the Members and the
 Chairperson would resolve certain matters which may better be delegated and, therefore, the arrangement for delegation
 is necessary to be made in law.  What matters may suitable be delegated and to whom, have been left for the decision of
 the Authority with in the scope and ambit of the legislation.   There is also an inbuilt safeguard under the provision of
 Clause 48 of the Bill that suitable conditions and limitations may be imposed by the Authority while delegating its
 powers.  A provision for delegation is necessary for efficient and convenient performance by the Authority consisting
 of number of persons for resolving the issues falling within their purview.    There is need to clearly demarcate policy
 and regulatory matters.
77.      The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed after taking into account its recommendations as enumerated
 in the preceding paragraphs.
78.      The Committee recommends that the Bill’s title should be changed from Airports Economic Regulatory
 Authority of India Bill, 2007 to Airports Economic Regulatory Authority of India Bill, 2008 as the year has changed
 from 2007 to 2008.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
Clause 2
The Committee notes that it will be critical in defining to what extent or what role a “stakeholder” such as
 an airline has in the key decision making processes of the regulatory framework.  The Committee feel that it is
 not clear from  the provisions of the Bill that whether the passengers using the airports would presumably be
 classified as one of the stakeholders so that they have the opportunity to make submission for determination of
 the quantum of the airport tariffs.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Bill should clearly define as
 to who are the principal stakeholders and establish unambiguously their role in the functioning of AERA and
 the consultative process for decision making by AERA.                                                              
                                                  (Para : 6)        
           
The Committee notes that cargo is one of the major components of the civil aviation sector and the omission of
 cargo from the definition of the Bill need to be rectified.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
 definition ‘airport user’ in Section 2(c) should read "as any person availing of passenger and/or cargo
 facilities".                                                                                                          
(Para :8)
            The Committee also received a representation stating that various surcharges imposed on the cargo added
 to more than what is the freight charges.  The Committee feels that this also needs to be looked
 into.                                                             
(Para : 9)
            The Committee recommends that the Ministry may suitably amend the Bill to include the cargo operators
 in the ambit of the Bill.                                             
(Para : 10)
            The Committee is of the opinion that the Members should also have the expertise on competition law and
 policy as the AERA is created to promote fair competition in the field of aviation.   Therefore, the Clause 4(2)
 may be amended accordingly.                                                                                                         (Para: 14)
            The Committee wonders whether in the Defence Forces there is any equal post to the Secretary.   The
 literal meaning of the clause does not bar personnel of the Defence Forces being appointed to the Authority. 
 However, in practice, the clause may effectively prevent the entry of experienced and meritorious people of the
 Defence Forces to the Authority.  Moreover, the reply of the Government gives an impression that the Authority
 can be filled up only by Members of bureaucracy.  In fact, in the era of economic liberalization and globalization
 a lot of talent and expertise is available outside the Government set up.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the
 law should be flexible not only to accommodate the personnel of the Defence Forces but also to accommodate the
 experts from the private sector.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Clause 4(2) may be suitably
 modified.              
(Para :15)
 
Clause 6
            The Committee notes the clarification furnished by the Ministry. The Committee, however, feels that to
 avoid ambiguity and multiplicity of interpretation it is better to define the aspects of reappointment in the clause
 itself.  While drafting the clause the legislative intent should be made amply clear.   Theoretically, it is possible
 that a Chairperson could be appointed as a Member, though normally it is not done.  Therefore, the Committee
 recommends that the clause should be modified in such a way making it clear that a Member cannot be
 appointed as Chairperson but a Chairperson can be appointed as a Member.                  
                                                                   (Para : 20)

Clause 13
The Committee observes that though the basic infrastructure of airport is geared towards providing
 landing, housing, parking of an aircraft along with supporting ground handling, navigation, surveillance and
 communication facilities, the airports also provide banks and other office spaces etc.  The economies of airport
 operation depends on both revenue streams i.e. aeronautical revenue and non-aeronautical revenue.  Even
 though the bulk of revenue for Indian airports come from aeronautical services, world over the successful
 airports get majority of their revenue from non-aeronautical services.                                                    
                                                                                                              (Para : 26)    
            The Committee further observes that the points raised by the stakeholders need serious consideration in
 view of the financial implication involved in it and the Government may amend the Bill in order to include non-
aeronautical service also in the ambit of the Bill.                                                                                                   
(Para : 27)
            The Committee feels that there appears to be a gap between the definitions of aeronautical services as
 defined in the AERA Bill and the coverage of aeronautical services under the concession agreement for airports
 signed by the Government of India or even the Operations Management Development Agreement, the OMDA
 signed in the case of Delhi and Mumbai airports.  The Committee is of the opinion that while the AERA Bill
 limits itself to the navigation, surveillance and supportive communication for Air Traffic Management and for
 landing, housing or parking of aircraft, the OMDA has a broader scope for aeronautical services and it includes
 baggage systems, check-in concourses and hydrant infrastructure for aircraft fuelling services among many
 others.  The Committee recommends that AERA oversight for aeronautical services and their charges should
 not be restrictive in scope, but should be extended to all other major aeronautical service heads laid out in
 concession and OMDA agreements as AERA has to ensure a balanced outcome between airports, airlines and
 also the passengers as many services which have been left out of AERA coverage are essential to passengers and
 need monitoring by a regulator.    The Committee welcomes the regulation of aeronautical services by the new
 regulator even though this will be only a small part of the revenue earning however, the non-aeronautical
 services, which are the large chunk of the earnings will go as un-regulated.   The ambit of AERA should be
 broadened to include regulation of both aeronautical, as well as, non-aeronautical revenue.  As per the current
 proposal, only aeronautical revenues are sought to be regulated through AERA.  The Committee recommends
 that this lacuna should be addressed by the Government and the non-aeronautical services also be brought
 under the ambit of proposed regulator.                                                                                    
                                                                                                                              (Para :29)
            The Committee strongly recommends that the fuel supply infrastructure should be brought under the
 purview of AERA Bill and this should be added in the powers and functions of the authority in Chapter 3 of the
 Bill.                                                
(Para : 31)
            The Committee observes that the Airports Authority of India, did not have any fixed performance
 standards to serve the passengers or to that matter for the efficiency of the airports.  The Bill presently covers
 only major airports handling 1.5 million or more passengers per annum.  The Committee does not find any
 reason to exclude about 116 odd other airports from the purview of the present Bill.   The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that the role of AERA and its functions should be expanded to cover all the airports used for the
 operation of commercial flights irrespective of the size of the airport or ownership or throughput of
 passengers.                                                         
(Para : 34)
            The Committee hopes that any amount of development fee which will be fixed by the AERA should not
 dampen the passenger demand.  The Committee is of the opinion that making air travel expensive by such
 development fees will have a significant impact on the overall economy, especially, on the tourism, commerce
 and hospitality sectors.  The Committee hopes that the proposed regulator will definitely play a positive and

REPORT
 
The Department of Shipping encompasses under its mandate Shipping and Port Sector, which include Shipbuilding and Ship-repair, Major Ports, National Waterways and Inland Water Transport. On a specific query about the efforts taken by the Department for addressing procedural hurdles for timely approval and execution of the projects, the Department informed that the procedure to be followed for formulation, appraisal and approval of projects to be funded through public investment and also for Public Private Partnership (PPP) projects have
 been laid down by the Ministry of Finance.   All such projects are required to be appraised by the appropriate Appraisal Forum [Standing Finance Committee (SFC), Departmental Expenditure Finance Committee (Departmental EFC), Main Expenditure Finance Committee (Main EFC), Committee of Secretaries (CoS), Public investment Board (PIB) or Public
 Private Partnership Appraisal Committee (PPPAC) as the case may be] depending upon the nature and estimated cost of the project before obtaining the approval of the Competent authority.   Further, Delegation of financial powers to the Port Trusts is a major policy instrument designed to address the procedural hurdles involved in approval of development
 projects in the Major Ports.  At present, financial powers for incurring expenditure upto Rs.50 crore in respect of new Plan projects and upto Rs.100 crore in respect of renewal / replacement projects included in the Plan for the Major Port Trusts have been delegated to the Port Trust Boards.  Recently, the M/o Finance have issued instructions whereby powers to
 sanction Plan projects upto Rs.75 crore have been delegated to the Minister-in-charge of the administrative Ministry and upto Rs.150 crore have been delegated to the ‘Minister-in-charge of the administrative Ministry and the Minister of Finance’.  Thus the threshold limit for obtaining approval of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs stands raised to
 Rs.150 crore from Rs.100 crore earlier.   The financial limits for appraisal of Plan projects by the Standing Committee on Finance, Expenditure Finance Committee and the Public Investment Board have also been suitably enhanced and rationalised. The threshold limit for appraisal of public private partnership projects (PPPs) by the Public Private Partnership
 Appraisal Committee (PPPAC) stands enhanced from Rs.100 crore earlier to Rs.250 crore.  Further, the new Model Concession Agreement for private sector projects in the Major Ports has been finalized.   New model ‘Request for Qualification’ (RFQ) and ‘Request for Proposal’ (RFP) documents have also been finalized.  This will enable the Major Ports to
 dispense with the need for obtaining ‘in-principle’ approval of PPPAC for even those PPP projects costing more than Rs. 250 crore as long as the bidding documents (i.e RFQ and RFP documents) and the   project agreements are in line with the above model documents.   The Major Ports have also been authorised to initiate the tendering action for selection of
 Project Management Consultants in anticipation of approval of the projects by the Competent Authority, subject to certain conditions with a view to saving time. Further, the requirement of obtaining ‘in-principle’ approval of the Planning Commission for inclusion of projects costing Rs. 50 crore and more in the Annual Plans has been dispensed with subject to
 the projects fulfilling certain conditions.

58.       The Committee has been drawing attention of the Government to the problem of multiplicity of taxes having adverse impact on shipping sector.
  The Government, however, till date has not come out with a proposal for rationalization and as of now there are twelve different taxes ailing the country’s shipping sector particularly the EXIM trade.  The
 Committee feels that Indian shipping will remain uncompetitive unless Government provides the level playing-field as available to other maritime nations in the world.  Since the shipping is truly international business with no commercial barrier, the Committee recommends that the Government must provide a level playing field by attempting to rationalize the
 tax structure and eliminate the disparity in tax treatment which counters the growth of the shipping sector and ultimately tonnage is losing out.  The Committee also recommends the Department to continue to make all out efforts at the highest level till the matter is favourably resolved.

INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
76.       Inland waterways comprising of rivers, lakes, canals, creeks, backwaters, etc. extend to about 14,500 kms. in India.  However, the true potential of this important mode of transport is yet to be exploited.
77.       Inland Water Transport (IWT) schemes mainly relate to development of waterways and augmentation of the traffic carrying capacity through expansion and modernization of IWT infrastructure/vessels.   Whereas the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) is responsible for the development of National Waterways, responsibility for the development
 of State Waterways rests with the State Governments. The Central Government has declared three Waterways, viz. Allahabad  – Haldia Stretch (1620 Kms.) Sadiya and Dhubri Stretch (891 kms.) and West Coast Canal from Kollam to Kottapuram stretch along with Udyogamandal Champakara canals (205 kms.) as National Waterways  and are being developed
 by IWAI for shipping and navigation by providing/maintaining basic IWT infrastructure i.e. fairway, navigational aids and terminals.  Three more waterways namely the Kakinada-Puducherry canals along with Godavari and Krishna rivers (1095 km), East Coast Canal along with Brahmani river and Mahanadi  delta (623 km) and Barak river (121 km) are under
 active consideration of the Govt for declaration as new National Waterways.
78.       In BE 2007-08, an outlay of Rs.158 crore which included Rs.75.90 crore for North-Eastern areas and Rs.82.10 crore for grants to IWAI was provided to the IWT sector.  This was reduced to Rs.138.60 crore at RE stage and an expenditure upto Febuary 2008 is Rs.56.53 crore and the anticipated expenditure upto March 2008 is Rs.107.73 crore.  During the
 Financial Year 2008-09, a sum of Rs.180.00 crore (including Rs.60.00 crore for NE Pool) has been earmarked towards Plan Support to IWAI. 
79.       Inland Water Transport Policy framework and strategy for development including guidelines for private investment in IWT sector have been approved by the Government.  These measures aim at helping IWAI to mobilize the required resources by attracting Private Investment and by forming Joint Ventures for developing Waterway Infrastructure &
 Cargo handling facilities.  To achieve a substantial step-up in IWT traffic, the thrust will therefore, be on the creation of infrastructure in the form of fairways with adequate depth and width besides setting-up of terminals and navigational aids.  An Inland Vessel Building Subsidy Scheme for providing 30% Subsidy for Inland Vessels built in Indian Shipyard and
 for operation on National Waterways was in existence from 1
st April, 2002 to 31.03.2007.  It is proposed to extend it for 10 years beyond 31.03.2007.
80.          IWT traffic operations are predominantly controlled by private entrepreneurs, particularly in Goa region.  The only public sector undertaking in the IWT sector, Central Inland Water Transport Corporation (CIWTC) operates traffic in the Eastern and North Eastern Region. Approximate share of organized IWT sector in the country in terms of tonne-km
 is a little over 0.30% of the total inland freight transportation. IWAI had engaged M/s IFCI Ltd as a consultant for identifying and processing private sector participation projects in IWT field.   The consultant had prepared some priority projects which were advertised in the market inviting bids.  After due process of bidding four Memorandum of Understanding
 (MOU)’s have been signed between IWAI and respective successful bidders for setting up and management of jetties at Bandel, Kolaghat and Budge-Budge in West Bengal and for acquisition, operation and management of barges on O-D pairs of Kolkata-Mongla, Kolkata-Dhubri and Kolkata-Pandu.  This process was in line with IWT Policy, 2001. Further
 steps for setting up of JVs are being taken.  A project Development Organisation/ Project Development Committee mechanism for identifying, developing and processing PPP projects has been finalized.  Besides, one cement company has been given land at Pandu port for developing terminal for handling clinker, cement etc to be transported by IWT mode. 
 Institutional arrangements for development of IWT are already in place.   Inland Waterways Authority of India is a Central Government agency primarily responsible for development and regulation of National Waterways for shipping and navigation.   Most of the riverine States however, do not have separate organizations to look after IWT sector and need to
 build the same.  Also, wherever IWT organizations are available in the States, these also need to be up graded/ strengthened.  
81.       The Committee has consistently expressed its concern over the slow pace of utilization of plan outlays and development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country. The Committee notes with anguish that an outlay of Rs.158.00 crore was allocated in BE 2007-08 for the IWT sector but it was reduced to Rs.138.60 crore at RE stage and an expenditure
 of Rs.56.53 crore was made only upto February, 2008.   The Committee is disappointed to note the continuous under utilization of funds by the Department of Shipping for development of IWT sector.  The Committee expects that the Department would make every endeavour to ensure that the measures adopted for the growth of IWT sector in the country is
 monitored scrupulously to achieve the envisaged physical and financial targets. 
82.       The Committee notes that potential of the  Inland Water Transport remains largely unexplored due to the indifferent attitude of the Central and State Governments. The Committee observes that although the Department of Shipping is committed to increase the share of Inland Water Transport in the country’s total EXIM trade, still the waterways are not
 being utilized to their potential and remain largely neglected and underdeveloped for want of required infrastructure namely fairways, terminals and navigable aids, as a result, it has not reached at a threshold level to become commercially viable. The Committee is of the view that with adequate investments, policy framework and focused approach, the Inland
 Water Transport in the country can be developed into a viable transport mode complementary to the rail and road modes. The Committee is of the opinion that to develop the Inland Water Transport sector with fast pace to its full potential in the country, the Government should endeavor to provide institutional framework and minimize the procedural bottlenecks
 besides providing adequate investments both from public and private partnership primarily public investment in Inland Water Transport and to develop it to a level where private sector feels confident to invest in this sector particularly in ownership and operation of cargo and passenger vessels to Inland Water Transport mode. The Committee, therefore,
 recommends the Government to provide institutional framework and basic infrastructural facility for accelerated development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country under National Maritime Development Programme.
83.       The Committee then enquired about the plan to increase the cargo movement on these national waterways.  The Department of Shipping informed the Committee that to increase the cargo movement on the three national waterways, IWAI has prepared on Action Plan for making the three national waterways fully functional at an estimated cost of
 Rs.751.00 crore subject to availability of funds. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for the dropped centrally sponsored scheme for development of IWT Sector; the Department of Shipping informed the Committee that for good economic development of any country the transport infrastructure is an extremely important factor.  Primarily there are three modes of transportation for bulk goods
 namely Rail, Road and Inland Water Transport (IWT).  However, while the rail and road modes developed significantly in the country, the IWT mode remained totally neglected due to which this mode lost its significance in the overall transport mix.  The development of inland waterways started with the formation of Inland Waterways Authority of India
 (IWAI) in October 1986.  However, as per constitutional provisions, only those waterways which are declared as National Waterways by Acts of Parliament can be developed by the Central Govt/IWAI.  The other waterways remain under the purview of the respective State Government.
 88.       For overall development of IWT sector it is necessary that not only the National Waterways but the other waterways (many of which are the feeder waterways to these National Waterways) should also be developed by providing IWT infrastructure.  Then only the total potential of IWT sector
 in the country can be exploited.  The importance of development of this mode  assumes greater significance considering that the IWT mode is a cost effective, environment friendly and fuel efficient mode of transport, especially for bulk cargo, over dimensional cargo and hazardous cargo, if adequate infrastructure is developed and maintained on all potential
 waterways.
89.       Most of the State Governments, however, suffer from financial constraints due to which development of IWT mode does not become a priority activity for them.  It is because of this factor that a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) which existed till March 2002 under which 50% financial assistance had been provided by the Central Government to
 respective States as a loan on reimbursement basis.  However, due to the above nature of the financial assistance this scheme was not very popular among the States and therefore, the funding pattern of CSS for IWT sector was modified in 2002 (guidelines of revised CSS issued in Nov. 2002) and 100% grant for North Eastern States and 90% grant for other
 States of the country was made available for taking up projects for IWT development by the States under CSS for IWT sector.
90.       This change in funding pattern encouraged several States for taking up different projects for development of IWT mode and during the 10th Plan period alone, 35 projects of 15 States costing Rs.107 crore were sanctioned by the DoS and central share of Rs.53 crore was also released to these States during the years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07.

95.       Under the Trade Agreement entered into between the Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and the Government of the Republic of India and the Protocol signed by both the countries on IWT Trade & Transit, IWAI is the nodal agency in issuing necessary permission for
 inland barges of Bangladesh and India for their movement across the country and undertaking loading/unloading operation at designated Ports of Call.  Checking of authorized/illegal transportation of men and materials (cargo) falls under the purview of Customs Department (for material) and Immigration Department (for men) and IWAI do not play any role in
 the same.  The above two authorities, at their respective check points, check and verify, if, the cargo carried by them and the men present on board the ship are as per the declared manifesto (certified by BIWTA, the nodal agency on Trade & Transit Protocol on behalf of Bangladesh Govt).  At all other points the Border Security Force keeps vigil on illegal
 immigrants/illegal movement of goods.  No security personnel is provided on Bangladeshi vessels by BSF/State Government/IWAI.  The crew of Bangladeshi vessels has to report to Customs and Immigration Department at their respective check points at the border for their verification and necessary entry.  Similarly, for outgoing vessels, the above details are
 again cross checked by Immigration/Customs Department.   The Government of West Bengal or Assam has never raised any issue regarding security problem due to plying of Bangladeshi vessels in Sunderbans/Protocol route.  Bangladeshi vessels never demanded from IWAI, security arrangement in their vessels nor have the State Government of West
 Bengal/Assam ever requested that security arrangement in Bangladeshi vessels be provided.  However, communications to the Government of West Bengal and Ministry of Home Affairs have been issued for comments in this regard. The reply is awaited.

 vessels on Kolkata/ Haldia- Narayanganj route are that Bangladeshi vessels are more economical in the tidal zone, they have lower cost of construction, less cost of manning and the bunker used by them is also cheaper. Though, there is a provision in the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade for sharing of cargo on 50:50 basis by Indian
 and Bangladeshi flag vessels, it is very difficult to enforce the same in view of the market forces and limitation of availability of Indian flag vessels.  However, this point is being raised with the Bangladesh authorities as and when discussion takes place with them.

HOOGHLY DOCK & PORT ENGINEERS LIMITED
            The Committee notes that a final cabinet note for Rehabilitation-cum-Restructuring Package is being finalized for according approval of CCEA.  The Committee also notes that a token provision of Rs.0.50 crore has been kept for revival package during 2008-09.  The Committee wishes the Government to grant an early approval for
 revival of HDPEL and write-off the Government loan and interest liability for improving the financial health of the company.  The Committee hopes that with the approval and implementation package, the company would achieve a turn around and earn sustainable profits.
(Para 75)
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
            The Committee has consistently expressed its concern over the slow pace of utilization of plan outlays and development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country. The Committee notes with anguish that an outlay of Rs.158.00 crore was allocated in BE 2007-08 for the IWT sector but it was reduced to Rs.138.60 crore at RE stage
 and an expenditure of Rs.56.53 crore was made only upto February, 2008.   The Committee is disappointed to note the continuous under utilization of funds by the Department of Shipping for development of IWT sector.  The Committee expects that the Department would make every endeavour to ensure that the measures adopted for the
 growth of IWT sector in the country is monitored scrupulously to achieve the envisaged physical and financial targets. 
(Para 81)
            The Committee notes that potential of the  Inland Water Transport remains largely unexplored due to the indifferent attitude of the Central and State Governments. The Committee observes that although the Department of Shipping is committed to increase the share of Inland Water Transport in the country’s total EXIM trade, still
 the waterways are not being utilized to their potential and remain largely neglected and underdeveloped for want of required infrastructure namely fairways, terminals and navigable aids, as a result, it has not reached at a threshold level to become commercially viable. The Committee is of the view that with adequate investments, policy
 framework and focused approach, the Inland Water Transport in the country can be developed into a viable transport mode complementary to the rail and road modes. The Committee is of the opinion that to develop the Inland Water Transport sector with fast pace to its full potential in the country, the Government should endeavor to
 provide institutional framework and minimize the procedural bottlenecks besides providing adequate investments both from public and private partnership primarily public investment in Inland Water Transport and to develop it to a level where private sector feels confident to invest in this sector particularly in ownership and operation of
 cargo and passenger vessels to Inland Water Transport mode. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to provide institutional framework and basic infrastructural facility for accelerated development of Inland Water Transport sector in the country under National Maritime Development Programme.
(Para 82)
            The Committee notes with dismay over the discontinuance of the centrally sponsored scheme for IWT development in the country by the Planning Commission.  The Committee is of the view that the decision of the Planning Commission to convert the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for IWT development into central sector
 scheme will adversely affect the pace of development of Inland Water Transport in the country.  The Committee recommends the Department of Shipping to impress upon the Planning Commission for the revival of the central sponsored scheme for overall development of the IWT Sector during the annual plan itself.
(Para 93)
            The Committee is constrained to note that cargo transportation by Inland Water Transport mode has not shown significant improvement on the three National Waterways.  The Committee also expresses its displeasure over the fact that no comparative cost-output evaluation for transportation of cargo through this inland water
 transport has been carried out by the Department.  The Committee is of the view that such evaluation would further establish the support of Inland Water Transport over other mode of transports.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that a detailed study should be carried out by the Department in this regard. The Committee also urges
 the Department to fix realistic physical target for cargo transportation by IWT mode year-wise for entire 11
th Plan period and put in place institutional monitoring mechanism for achieving the desired growth.
(Para 94)
CENTRAL INLAND WATER TRANSPORT CORPORATION
            The Committee notes with anguish that no security personnel are being provided for safe transportation of men and material in Suderbans/Protocol routes in West Bengal.   The Committee is of the opinion that security is a prime concern and should be looked into seriously by making commensurate security arrangement in
 Suderbans/Protocol routes.  The Committee recommends the Department of Shipping to take up the matter of beefing-up of security arrangement in the Suderbans/Protocol routes with the Union Home Ministry so that inadequacy of police deployment could be addressed in a big way.
(Para 97)
            The Committee is pained to note that the Government has decided neither to consider revival of CIWTC nor to amalgamate this Corporation with various Organizations, such as Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) or Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) that too, without getting conducted any
 scientific study by an expert agency.  The Committee is of the view that the matter of revival and amalgamation of CIWTC should be got examined by some high powered expert committee.    The Committee once again reiterates its earlier recommendation contained in 117 th Report on Demands for Grants 2007-08 of Department of
 Shipping, which is reproduced below:
“The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of its recommendation in the past, the Government has not come out with a complete blueprint for making full use of the existing assets of River Service Division (RSD). The Committee is of the opinion that CIWTC with its infrastructure and expertise can play an integral part
 for development and promotion of inland water transport through NW-I and NW-II. The Committee recommends that possibility may also be explored to physically amalgamate the remaining CIWTC with Inland Water Transport Authority of India (IWAI) or Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) or Shipping Corporation of India
 (SCI), so that the infrastructure and expertise of CIWTC can be utilized for development of waterways transport.”
(Para 100)
DEVELOPMENT OF WATER TRANSPORT IN ANDAMAN & NICOBAR AND LAKSHADWEEP ISLANDS
            The Shipping Corporation of India with its two owned passenger-cum-cargo vessels and 27 managed vessels operates domestic passenger-cum-transportation services between mainland and Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep group of islands on behalf of the Government of India.  Presently, Andaman and Nicobar Island
 administration has 22 vessels comprising of 18 passenger vessels and 4 passenger-cum-cargo vessels, Union Territory of Lakshdweep has 5 vessels comprising 1 passenger-cum-cargo vessel, 3 passenger vessels and one bunker barge.  The Committee observes that water transport is the life-line of these groups of islands for their
 interconnection with the mainland and within islands.  The Committee notes that this sector has been neglected for so many years without any fund infusion for modernization of the vessels and purchase of additional vessels.  Due to this, the populations of these islands are suffering to a great extent.  The Committee further notes that in the
 Demand-for-Grants for the year 2008-09 no financial allocation has been made for improving the interconnectivity and water transport in Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshdweep islands.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Government of India to take immediate steps for improving inter-islands connectivity of the
 islands of Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshdweep for mitigating the problems of connectivity between these islands.  The Committee also recommends that sufficient Budgetary Allocation may be provided for augmenting the water transport connectivity in these islands.
(Para 101)

1
REPORT
The Department of Road Transport and Highways under the Ministry of Shipping, Road
Transport and Highways has been entrusted primarily with the functions of construction and
maintenance of National Highways (NH), administration of Motor V ehicle Act and Central Motor
Vehicles Rules, formulation of broad policies relating to road transport, environmental issues,
relating to vehicular movements automotive norms, etc. besides making arrangements for
movements of vehicular traffic with neighbouring countries.
2. India has a vast road network of 3.32 million km. of which the National Highways and
the State Highways together account for 1,95,000 kms. The length of National Highways
network is only 66754 kms. (at present) constituting about 2 per cent of the total road network
in the country and carrying about 40 per cent of the total traffic across the length and breadth
of the country. The number of vehicles has been growing at a rapid pace of 12 per cent per
annum and consequently traffic on the roads is growing at 7-10 per cent per annum. The share
of roads in total traffic has been growing from 12 per cent of freight traffic and 31.6 per cent
of the passenger traffic in 1950-51 to a projected 65 per cent of freight traffic and 87 per cent
of passenger traffic.
3. To cope with this increase, appropriate expansion and improvement of the road network
is necessary. All this requires a massive infusion of funds. Historically, investments in roads,
especially highways, were mainly made by the Government because of the large volume of
resources required, long gestation period of projects, uncertain returns and various associated
externalities. But in recent times, the private sector has been actively involved in the development
and maintenance of the National Highways. The Ministry has formulated policy guidelines to
encourage private sector participation in the highway sector, besides providing several incentives
such as tax exemptions and duty free import of road building equipment and machinery. Model
Concession Agreements have also been finalized for major road projects.
4. The Road Transport Wing of the Department is concerned with the formulation of broad
policies related to road transport besides making provisions for the movement of vehicular traffic
with the neighbouring countries. The following Acts/Rules which embody the policy relating to
motor vehicles and State Transport Corporations are being administered in the Road Transport
Wing of the Department:—
• The Motor V ehicles Act, 1988
• The Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989
• The Road Transport Corporations Act, 1950
• The Carriers Act, 1865
5. The development and maintenance of National Highways are being done on agency basis.
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), State Public Works Departments (PWDs) and
the Border Roads Organisation are the main agencies. Out of the total National Highways length
of 66754 km, about 19706 km. have been entrusted to National Highways Authority of India
(NHAI) for improvement under National Highway Development Project (NHDP), and some other
non NHDP scheme. About 46050 km. length of National Highways is at present entrusted to
State PWDs and Border Road Organisation (BRO) as agencies of the Ministry and about 998 km.
length are yet to be entrusted.

2
6. Our country having one of the largest road networks of 3.32 million km., consists of
expressways, National Highways, State Highways, Major District Roads, Other District Roads and
Village Roads with following length distribution:
National Highways/Expressways : 66754 km.
State Highways : 128000 km.
Major and other District Roads : 470000 km.
Rural Roads : 2650000 km.
7. The National Highways have further been classified depending upon the width formation.
Generally, a lane has a width of 3.75 metres in case of single lane and 3.5 metres in case of
multi lane National Highways. The break-up of National Highways in terms of width is as under:

26. The Committee notes that the growth of Motor Vehicles in India is unprecedented.
The process of liberalization and globalization augmented the number of vehicles to
beyond the imagination of our planners of road sector development. The infrastructure
available is not at all commensurate with the growth of vehicles. The Committee also
notes that the allocation to the Department is almost static in real terms. There is an
increase of 20 per cent in Annual Plan outlay and 7.6 per cent in budgetary support. The
above increase in Annual Plan outlay and budgetary support may not be adequate even
to meet the increase in cost. Thus, it poses a great mismatch between the availability of
the road infrastructure and vehicular population.
27. Inadequate development of road sector will result in congested roads, traffic jams,
recurring accidents and chaos in the road sector. Moreover, the development of road
infrastructure is immensely important to sustain the growth of the economy. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should allot funds to the
Department of Road Transport and Highways so as to ensure the development of road
infrastructure in proportion to the growth of vehicles. The Committee further
recommends that demands of the Department may be acceded to at the RE stage.

non-furnishing of utilization certificates thereof, the scope of the scheme was amended in 2000-
2001 to provide equipment instead of cash grant. NGOs were also included under the ambit of
the Scheme. During 2007-08, 30 cranes and 100 ambulances are expected to be provided to
States/UTs/NGOs.
74. The Committee found that the performance of the Department on this particular area is
very much disappointing. A target of provision of 50 cranes and 100 ambulances was fixed for
the year 2007-08. However, an analysis of the performance of the Department for the first nine
months of 2007-08 reveals that so far tender bids for ambulance have technically evaluated and
the financial bids have been opened and the file is being processed before placing work order.
Regarding the purchase of cranes is concerned, the Department stated that the file is under
submission before the Hon’ble Minister for seeking approval for placing work order for supply
of cranes. The Committee also raised this issue during the deliberations of the Secretary,
Department of Road Transport and highways and expressed its concern over the non-availability
of trauma centres on the national highways for which the Secretary responded:
“... For this, the Health Ministry has approved a project of setting up 140 trauma centres
at a cost of about Rs.750 crores; and we will provide ambulances, which are
well-equipped, for all these 140 trauma centres. Each ambulance will cost about
Rs.15-20 lakhs but we will go by whatever the Health Ministry says. In addition to this,
in the National Highways, being developed under the NHDP, in every 50 kilometres, there
will be an ambulance”.
75. The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department for providing
trauma care. At the very same time the Committee feels that the present allocation of
fund of Rs. 22.20 crore for the trauma care is too inadequate. The Government should
try to augment the funding for trauma care. The Committee is constrained to note the
tardy progress made in purchasing cranes and ambulances. The Committee also
recommends that the formalities for purchasing cranes and ambulances may be completed
at the earliest so that the trauma care facilities can be put in place without further delay.

78. Application of information technology for the development of the country is the mantra
of the day. Of course, the Department has taken initiatives in the right direction way back in
the year 2001. The Committee notes that till now only a few states have embarked on the

have the resources, talent and expertise in the IT field. The Committee wonders what prevent
the Government from implementing the IT enabled systems in the Road Transport Sector. The
Committee notes that target for completion of the IT enabled systems is 2009 which is not far
away. The Committee has doubt whether the Government will be able to meet the target which
they could not do for the last seven years. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
matters may be reviewed at the highest level and steps may be taken to remove the
bottlenecks. The Committee also recommends that those States which are not
implementing the IT enabled Driving Licence and Registration Certificate may be
persuaded highlighting the benefit and importance of IT enabled system for DL and RC.
The Committee also recommends that some incentive scheme may be developed in such
a way that those States which are implementing the IT enabled systems should get
sanction for more projects and schemes.

83. The Department informed the Committee that under Section 59 of the M.V . Act, 1998
Central Government has powers to fix the age of motor vehicles of different categories.
However, as yet this Section has not been invoked. We have only fixed the ‘age’ of certain
categories of vehicles for the purpose of tourist permit and national permit, under rule 82 and
88 of CMVR, 1989. This Ministry’s stand has been that a well maintained older vehicle can be
less polluting than an ill maintained newer vehicle. A vehicle can ply on the road as long as it
meets the requirements of the Motor Vehicles Act and Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 with
regard to safety, emission and fitness norms. Fixation of age of vehicle would also be not
advisable keeping in view the socio-economic conditions of the country.
84. The Department further stated that a transport vehicle has to undergo fitness test every
year after two years of the date of initial registration. There is no such requirement for non-
transport vehicle for 15 years once they are registered. Hence the Department was of the
considered view that proper inspection and maintenance system must be put in place to identify
the vehicles which do not meet the emission and safety norms. Such inspection and maintenance
centres would need to be set up in various states with Public Private Partnership. During the
year 2008-09, allocation of Rs.7.00 crore has been made under the scheme.
85. The Committee welcomes the intention of the Government to set up more

regulatory authority should be put in place before these centres become operational as
there is a possibility that these centres can harass the vehicle owners in connivance with

86. When the Committee enquired about the steps taken to the strengthening of public
transport system, the Department replied that decline of public transport has been one of the
failures of our transport planning over the years. The percentage of buses in the total fleet of
vehicles has come down from more than 11 per cent in 1951 to 1.1 per cent in 2004. This
leads to increase in the personalized transport which in turn has a number of adverse
consequences such as congestion, pollution, and accidents apart from being in equalitarian as the
poor get excluded from transport services. This needs to be reversed. It is proposed that in the
Eleventh Five Year Plan the provisions should be made at the Central level to provide financial
assistance to help the States to strengthen their public transport system including application of
IT like automatic fare collection system based on GPS. However such financial assistance shall
be restricted to those States who undertake to take measures for reforms in the pubiic transport
system. An MOU between the Central Government and the State Governments embodying a
number of reform requirements such as rationalization of taxes in favour of public transport,
level playing field between the private and public operators, freedom in the matter of fare
fixation, improvement in the basic infrastructure, professional management of STUs etc. is to be
signed.
87. The Central Government could provide outright grant to such States by linking the
achievement of the reform agenda measurable by verifiable indices of increased provision and
usage of public transport. It could also provide guarantee to resource mobilisation by the States
for investment in public transport including renewal and augmentation of bus fleet. During the
year 2008-09, Rs.24.99 crore has been allocated for this purpose.
88. The Committee in its 84th and 102nd Reports recommended the Department to give more
importance to develop public transport and to discourage excessive use of private vehicles on the
roads. The Department responded that this issue was taken up with all the State Governments.
When the Committee asked about the reaction of the State Governments in this regard and the
action taken by Department to promote the public transport, the Department replied that the
views of the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee relating to improving public
transport system were brought to the notice of the State Governments especially with a request
to review and rationalize the tax structure. Response from only a few State Governments/UTs
was received. However, looking at the importance of the matter this department is in the process
of finalizing a broad scheme to provide central assistance to the State Government/UTs to
strengthen their public transport system. Under the proposed scheme, only those State
Governments would be entitled to receive the financial assistance who would undertake to carry
out certain reform measures for the benefit of the public transport system. A budget outlay of
Rs.24.99 crore has been proposed in the year 2008-09 for this purpose. Under the reform

20
measures the conditions such as rationalization of taxation in favour of public transport system
is also proposed to be included in the broad scheme.
89. The Committee is very much disappointed about the negligence on the part of the
Government in promoting public transport system in the country. The Committee is of the
opinion that cities are jammed with rising number of private vehicles and the villages are
not even getting adequate public transport facility. The Committee once again reiterates
its earlier recommendation that in the absence of user-friendly public transports, the
people in the country are resorting to excessive use of private vehicles and this has put
the roads under undue pressure. The Committee observes that most of the investment on
roads is being extracted from the public itself but the returns accruing to the users are
not equitable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the efforts of the Government
should focus on developing public transport, which discourages excessive use of private
vehicles. The Government should adopt a methodology, whereby, in the more densely
populated states, the rich and the affluent are asked to pay more for keeping more than
one vehicle.
CREATION OF NATIONAL ROAD SAFETY BOARD
90. The Committee was informed that the Committee on Road Safety and Traffic
Management constituted under the Chairmanship of Shri S. Sundar, Former  Secretary of erstwhile
M/o Surface Transport and Distinguished fellow, TERI has submitted its report to Hon’ble
Minister, S,RT and H on 20.2.2007. The Committee has recommended creation of a National
Road Safety Board under a separate Act of the Parliament. A note in this regard has been sent
to Cabinet Secretariat on 10.1.08. Since there is long way to go for constitution of this Board,
it has been proposed to allocate a token amount i.e. Rs.0.01 crore under this head for the year
2008-09.
91. When the Committee expressed its disappointment over the delay in the establishment of
National Road Safety and Traffic Board, the Secretary responded:
“.....What they have recommended is based on experience in other countries where road
safety is really given a very high priority. What they have said is really practical and
perhaps will be an effective way of handling the issue. Normally, what happens is these
Boards are set up, but there is no source of funding. They are suggesting one percent
Cess to be earmarked for road safety. For that they are suggesting amendment to the
Central Road Fund also. That is perhaps the right way. In there functions and duties all
this included”.
92. The Committee feels that the time has come for the creation of the much talked
about National Road Safety Board as the number of road accidents on national highways
is increasing in an alarming manner. The Committee recommends that the Department
should pursue the matter vigorously and take necessary actions to establish this Board at
the earliest.
TOLL TAX ON BRIDGES AND NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
93. The issue of collection of toll tax on bridges and national highways was raised by the
Committee during the course of evidence by the Secretary, Department of Road Transport and
Highways. The Committee in its 67th and 118th reports discussed the subject in detail and
recommended that once the cost of construction of a roadlbridge plus interest is recovered, the
collection of toll should be stopped. The Committee also felt that there exists a need for the
rationalisation of the toll tax being charged on the National Highways. To a specific

21
recommendation of the Committee in its 118th Report for creation of one time revolving fund,
the Department replied that present levy of cess is tied up for the implementation of NHDP and
Prime Minister’s Gram Sadak Yojana and the improvement of sanctioned works of State Road.
Therefore, it may not be possible to create a revolving fund until and unless the amount of cess
is increased. However, this is being taken up with Ministry of Finance.
94. The Committee once again recommends that once the capital and interest is
recovered, the users’ fee must be discontinued. The Committee is of the opinion that
there is a need for establishment of a regulator to determine the reasonable return to
the investor on road projects which is being considered as a yardstick for fixation of toll.
The Committee appreciates that in view of the resource crunch being faced by the
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and there is a genuine need for generation of
additional revenue by the Ministry. Whenever any National Highway is constructed, it
leads to huge value addition to the land adjoining the National Highway and these benefits
of addition in value have so far  been enjoyed by private agencies only. The Government
should also get advantage of the appreciation of land value because it is the taxpayer’s
money that has led to the value addition of that property. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government may explore the possibility of imposing some cess/tax
on land adjoining National Highways which is being utilized for commercial purpose on
annual basis. This could serve as a permanent source of income for the Government and
the revenue so generated could be ploughed back for the construction and maintenance
of National Highways in the country. Provision of ducting at the time of construction of
National Highways for laying telephone and electric cables also leads to value addition and
can be explored for generating more funds for the road sector. These measures may go
a long way to meet the resource gap for maintenance and construction of National
Highways in the country.

ANNUAL PLAN 2007-08
The Committee observed that out of the RE (2007-08) Plan allocation
of Rs.14066.00 crore, an amount of Rs.11887.44 was spent (provisional) up to
12th March, 2008 which stands at 84.5 per cent of RE. The overall expenditure profile of
the Department is also not showing any encouraging trends. Out of Rs.16481.85 crore
(RE) for the year 2007-08, a sum of Rs.13338.03 crore was expended (provisional) till the
12th March, 2008 which stands at 81.0 per cent of the RE. This is very much in contrast
to the quantum of expenditure incurred in the year 2006-07 where it stood at a good
97.9 per cent of RE allocated for that year. (Para 11)
The Committee finds that despite its earlier recommendations on the aspect of
funds utilization and the need for constant monitoring of projects, the Department of
Road Transport and Highways has done pr ecious little to improve the situation. This is
evident from the reply of the Department with regard to non-utilisation of funds that the
allocation for road sector is based on anticipated implementation of projects every year.
The Committee is of the opinion that the road sector plays a vital role in providing good
infrastructure in the country. The Committee feels that submission of routine replies for
under utilization of funds and poor performance in achieving the physical targets is not
going to yield any result. Instead of that the Department may list out the bottlenecks and
draw a strategy to overcome such bottlenecks. The Committee is of the opinion that
active involvement of project executing agencies such as PWD, NHAI and State
Governments would only help the Department in utilizing its fund to the maximum
extent. The Committee, therefore, recommends that proper co-ordination with all these
organizations should be maintained in order to achieve physical targets satisfactorily.
(Para 15)
ANNUAL PLAN 2008-09
The Committee notes that the growth of Motor Vehicles in India is unprecedented.
The process of liberalization and globalization augmented the numbet of vehicles to
beyond the imagination of our planners of road sector development. The infrastructure
available is not at all commensurate with the  growth of vehicles. The Committee also
notes that the allocation to the Department is almost static in real terms. There is an
increase of 20 per cent in Annual Plan outlay and 7.6 per cent in budgetary support. The
above increase in Annual Plan outlay and budgetary support may not be adequate even
to meet the increase in cost. Thus, it poses a great mismatch between the availability of
the road infrastructure and vehicular population, Inadequate development of road sector
will result in congested roads, traffic jams, recurring accidents and chaos in the road
sector. Moreover, the development of road infrastructure is immensely important to
sustain the growth of the economy. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should allot funds to the Department of Road Transport and Highways so as
to ensure the development of road infrastructure in proportion to the growth of vehicles.
The Committee further recommends that demands of the Department may be acceded to
at the RE stage. (Para 26 & 27)

Report
The tourism has been a major social phenomenon of the societies all along.  It is motivated by the natural urge of every
 human being for new experience, adventure, education and entertainment.  Tourism is a multi sectoral activity characterized by
 multiple services provided by a range of suppliers.  It is largest service industry in the country.  Its importance lies in being an
 instrument for economic development and employment generation.   The tourism has been pivotal in social progress as well as
 an important vehicle of widening socio-economic and cultural contacts throughout human history.  A wide array of interests-
entertainment, sports, religion, culture,  adventure, education, health and business- drives tourism through increased contact.   It
 helps to promote cultural cohesion and social bonding and creates a durable social fabric.  With the advancement of transport,
 communication and improvement in general economic well being the demand for tourism has increased manifold.   The Five-
Year Plan perspective initiatives required for the development of tourism synergize with the development efforts needed to
 accomplish a number of other goals like employment generation, advancement of women and disadvantaged groups.  The
 Government plays a crucial role in making provision for tourism infrastructure and skill development. Such initiatives
 catalyses private enterprises to come forward and invest in this sector.  The share of India in international tourist arrival
 continues to increase from 2004 onwards.  But the share is still low at 0.55% in 2007.  The foreign tourist arrival rose from
 3.46 million in 2004 to an estimated 5 million in 2007.  Further more, foreign exchange earnings from tourism in India rose
 substantially from US$3 billion in 2002 to an estimated US$ 11.96 billion in 2007.  The share of India in world’s tourism
 receipts scaled from 0.65 per cent in 2002 to 1.21 percent in 2006. 
2.         The Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and programmes and for the
 coordination of activities of various Central Government agencies, State Governments/Union Territories and the Private Sector
 for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The Ministry of Tourism plays a crucial role in coordinating and
 supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territories Governments, catalyzing private investment, strengthening
 promotional and marketing efforts and in providing trained manpower resources. The function of the Ministry of Tourism
 mainly consists of the following:-
·
        Framing of policy matters on development of tourism
·        Grant of Central Financial Assistance to States/UTs for Development of Tourism Infrastructure
·        Encouragement of Public Private participation in tourism infrastructure development
·        Promotion and marketing of Tourism Products within the country and abroad
·        Providing incentives in the accommodation sector
·        Regulation of tourism industry
·        Investment facilitation
·        Human Resource Development and Training
·        Research, analysis, monitoring and evaluation
·        International Cooperation of promotion and development of India Tourism
3.         The administrative head of the Ministry is the Secretary (Tourism).  The Secretary also acts as the Director General
 (DG) Tourism. The office of the Director General of Tourism {now merged with the office of Secretary (Tourism)} provides
 executive directions for the implementation of various policies and programmes.  Directorate General of Tourism has a field
 formation of 20 offices within the country and 13 offices abroad and one sub-ordinate office/project i.e. Indian Institute  of
 Skiing and Mountaineering (IISM)/Gulmarg Winter Sports Project (GWSP). The activities of IISM/GWSP have been revived
 and various ski and other courses are conducted in the J&K valley.  In addition to the Headquarters Organization at New Delhi,
 the Directorate General of Tourism has 20 India Tourism Offices including 5 Regional Offices, situated at New Delhi,
 Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata , Guwahati and other offices are located at Agra, Bhubaneswar, Aurangabad, Bangalore, Kochi,
 Hyderabad, Imphal, Jaipur, Khajuraho, Naharlagun, Panaji (Goa), Patna, Port Blair, Shillong and Varanasi.  There are 13 India
 Tourism Offices Overseas, which include 5 Regional Offices at, New York, Frankfurt, Dubai, Sydney and Tokyo.  The other
 India tourism Offices are located at Los Angeles, Toronto, London, Paris, Amsterdam, Milan, Johannesburg and Singapore.
 The overseas offices are primarily responsible for tourism promotion and marketing in their respective areas and the field
 offices in the country are responsible for providing information service to tourists and to monitor the progress of field projects. 
 4.        The Ministry of Tourism has the following public sector undertaking and autonomous institutions under its
 administrative control namely :
            (i)        India Tourism Development Corporation  Ltd.(ITDC);
(ii)       Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management    (IITTM);

8.         When asked about the projected demand of the Ministry of Tourism for 11th Five Year Plan and the allocation made for
 the entire Plan, the Ministry of Tourism in their replies submitted that the projected demand for eleventh Plan of the Ministry
 of Tourism was   Rs.5405.58 crore (10% basis) and Rs. 6569.61 crore (20% basis) The Planning Commission has allocated
 Rs.5156.00 crore. The requirement of additional funds could be considered at the time of mid term appraisal of the 11 th Plan. 
 Further in the annual plan 2008-09, the Ministry of Tourism projected its demand for Rs.1062.85 crore and the Planning
 Commission has allocated Rs.1000.00 crore.  The major activities/schemes of the Ministry of Tourism is for Tourist
 infrastructure augmentation, Development of Human Resource for hospitality and travel trade, Promotion and Publicity,
 Creating budget accommodation etc. for which Rs. 1000 crore have been allocated in B.E. 2008-09 for Ministry of Tourism. 
 All the schemes have been continued except the equity contribution to ITDC.
9.         The Committee observes that the Ministry of Tourism projected a requirement of Rs.5405.58 crore (10% basis) and Rs.
 6569.61 crore (20% basis) for the entire 11
th Plan against this requirement, the Planning Commission approved an allocation
 of Rs.5156.00 crore for carrying out major activities of the Ministry viz. Augmentation of Tourist infrastructure, Development
 of Human Resource for hospitality and travel trade, Promotion and Publicity, Creating budget accommodation etc.   The
 Committee also notes that in the Annual Plan 2008-09 the Ministry has projected an outlay of Rs.1062.85 crore against which
 an amount of  Rs.1000.00 crore was allocated.  The Committee deplores the tendency of Planning Commission and Ministry of
 Finance for imposing cuts on the amounts demanded by the Ministry.  This mismatch between projected amount and
 sanctioned outlay may result in widening further the gap between the tourism potential and development of tourism synergies
 for achieving the goals.   The Committee feels that in order to attain the National growth targets in the 11 th Plan Period, huge
 planned funding is required.  Thus, the Government spending for the Ministry of Tourism will have to be significantly stepped-
up from the present level to meet the investment targets.   The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of
 Tourism should be provided with Rs.6569.61 crore (20% basis) by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance for
 the 11 th Plan Period as per their original demand.    The Committee also recommends the Ministry of Tourism to take
 appropriate caution and remedial action to absorb in time the allocation made to them.

 high rate and can ensure consequential development of the infrastructure of the destinations and circuits.  The Committee feels

 and destinations needs to be carefully selected on the basis of their potential to provide all infrastructural  facilities  required by
 the tourists within such destinations and circuits.   The Committee is of the opinion that, if, India has to exploit its vast inherent
 potential  in tourism, then it must provide exclusive quality tourism product and destinations comparable with other Asian

 infrastructure, therefore, a lot of information dissemination is required in addition to hospitality and the scope and reach of the
 domestic tourism should also be broadened through development of these competitive destinations and circuits.   The
 Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to develop quality tourism at identified tourist circuits and destinations with
 focus on mega destinations and circuits that match international standards and satisfy the domestic and international tourists.

 Indian tourism products.   The Committee also urges the Ministry that while selecting a destination or a circuit they should
 attach priority for harmonious growth and development of all the Regions and States.

62.       The foreign tourists visit to India are subsided to a numbers of restrictions in the form of PAP/RAP/ILP for visiting the

 about the impact of abolition of permit system on the growth of foreign tourist arrivals in India and how it would help in
 exploiting the tourism potential of these islands optimally.   The Ministry of Tourism informed the          Committee that the
 PAP/RAP/ILP act as a hindrance to the growth and development of domestic and International tourism to these regions. The
 Government of India is providing Central Financial Assistance to these States for development of infrastructure which would
 be appropriately utilized when there is a mass flow of tourists to these regions. This would also result in giving a boost to the
 economy of the North Eastern States as well as in creation of jobs for the local population. The honorable Members of
 Parliament from the North – Eastern States have also raised this issue in the Consultative Committee and the Standing
 Committee on Transport, Tourism & Culture as even Indian citizens are also required to obtain permits to visit these areas.

 to unethical practices at the issuing level, at times.

 requirement of these permits. The Home Secretary, Government of India vide
 his letter dated September 22, 2006 has informed

 Affairs has been requested to expedite the review of these regulations with the respective State Governments.

 the requirement of permit system in the country as the growth of international tourism is based on development of tourism in

 visit the country specially the North Eastern States and Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands.  The restrictions on
 foreigners to stay beyond permitted period and visiting only selected islands/regions/destination has discouraged the foreign
 tourists arrival in the country.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to optimally exploit the potential of
 tourism in these islands/regions/destination, the restrictions on the foreigners on visiting the islands/regions may be removed

 Highways requiring improvement/upgradation.

 of accessibility and road connectivity to many destinations and tourism monuments.  The Ministry of Tourism has mooted
 specific proposals to the Department of Road Transport and Highways for better connectivity of National Highways and State
 Highways as well as construction of roads to World Heritage Sites and Buddhist sites.  The Department of Road Transport and
