6. The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the
outlay approved during 2007-08. This looks something strange at time when the civil
aviation sector is witnessing an unprecedented growth for past few years. The Ministry
anticipates to utilize an amount of Rs.11211.61 crore only out of the approved allocation
of Rs.12347.09 crore during the year 2007-08, which exemplifies the poor financial
management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The Committee feels that there is a lack
of proper planning in the various organisations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a result
of which the Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress
upon the concerned agencies to make a realistic assessment of their financial
requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized.
BUDGET 2008-09 AND ANNUAL PLAN FOR 2008-09
7. The Annual Plan outlay of the Ministry for the year 2008-09 is Rs.10031.00 crore.
8. To a specific query on the impact of Union Budget 2008-09 on the Civil Aviation sector
in the country and also about the incentives and concessions which have been announced in the
Union Budget 2008-09 for civil aviation sector, the Ministry replied that up to the financial year
2006-07, Section 10 (I5-A) of the Income Tax Act provided tax exemption on lease rentals for
lease of imported aircraft and aero engines This provision has not been continued in the Union
Budget 2008-09 and accordingly, lease of imported aircrafts and aero engines will be taxed at
rates ranging between 10 per cent and 40 per cent + surcharge etc. This makes leasing of
imported aircraft and aero engines more expensive and would adversely affect the financial health
of the aviation sector as leasing is an option exercised by many airlines in India. In terms of
concessions/initiatives, import of simulators for helicopters along with spares has been exempted
from Customs Duty in the Union Budget 2008-09.
9. The Ministry was further asked about the projected demand of the Ministry for the year
2008-09 and whether there has been any cut in its demand, if so, what was the reason extended
and which are the projects/schemes that might be affected by this cut. The Ministry replied
that for the Annual Plan 2008-09 projections in respect of Ministry of Civil Aviation was
Rs.10170.27 crores, including budgetary support of Rs.328.94 crores. Against this projection,
Planning Commission approved an outlay of Rs.10031.00 crores including budgetary support of
Rs.190.00 crores for 2008-09. Planning Commission, however, has not indicated any reason for
this cut. The scheme for setting up of Greenfield Airport at Pakyong, Sikkim will be affected
by this cut as the approved budgetary support component of Rs.190.00 crores does not include
the outlay of Rs.45.00 crores proposed to be given as grant for the scheme at Sikkim.

compared to the previous year, the Ministry replied that the Tenth Five Year Plan outlay was
Rs.12,2928 crores with a budgetary support component of Rs.400 crores. As against this, the
Eleventh Plan proposes Rs.55,302 crores with a budgetary support of Rs.1360.13 crores. This
quantum jump of more than four times is a clear indicator of the high growth potential and the
significance of the sector in the overall scheme of economic development. As for the financial
year 2008-09, the Plan outlay is Rs.10,031 crores which is almost one-fifth of the total five year
outlay.
11. The Committee feels that reduction in Budgetary support of the Ministry will

at Pakyong, Sikkim. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take this issue
with the Finance Ministry at RE stage and prevail upon them to grant more money to
ensure that works for project start well in time. The Committee expects that the
Government will ensure that the targets set for internal and extra budgetary resources
as well as external commercial borrowings from foreign banks/financial institutions for
bridging the gap in budgetary support will materialize. The Committee recommends that
the Ministry should take adequate steps during 2008-09 also to ensure optimum utilisation

18. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the erstwhile Air India had suffered
a provisional net loss (after tax) of Rs.447.93 crore during the year 2006-07 as against a net
profit of Rs.14.94 crore for the year 2005-06. The Ministry in its reply to the query on the
reasons for the loss has stated that this is due to settlement of wage arrears to the tune of
Rs.425 crores, decrease in load factor and fall in yield due to competition. The Ministry has also
informed that the passenger load factor has declined from 66.2 per cent to 63.8 per cent for
the year 2006-07.
19. The Committee was further informed by the Ministry that the erstwhile Indian
Airlines Limited had suffered a provisional net loss (after tax) of Rs.240.29 crore during the year
2006-07 as against a net profit of Rs.49.50 crore for the year 2005-06. The Ministry in its reply
to the query on the reasons for the loss has stated that the varied price of ATF is one of the
main causes for the loss. The Ministry also replied that on the revenue front also airlines
continued to be hit by rapidly declining passenger revenue yields on account of intense
competition and deployment of excess capacity in the market. Further, the bottom line of the
company was affected due to the writing off of the entire amount due from its subsidiary
company Airline Allied Services Limited (AASL) However, the passenger load factor has increased
from 71.6 per cent to 73.1 per cent for the year 2006-07.
20. The Committee desired to know the details of the steps taken to increase the profit/
passenger load factor of the Air India (new brand name) as the passenger load factor has a
direct impact on the profit or loss of the newly created NACIL. The Ministry in its reply stated
that the phased induction of new aircraft in the ageing fleet of Air India will have a very positive
impact in its operations. The Ministry has further stated that Purchase of 111 state-of-the-art
new aircraft with in-flight entertainment system, Refurbishment of existing aircraft with new
seats, Membership of Star Alliance, Rationalisation of schedules to eliminate overlapping of
flights, Streamlining of operations, implementation of free flow code share, Joint participation in

6
all schemes/promotions on domestic sectors, through check-in and seamless transfer at Mumbai,
Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata, Bangalore and Hyderabad where by passengers can connect domestic
flight to an international flight in a single check-in process, Introduction of non-stop flights from
Mumbai and Delhi to New York, Mumbai to Hong Kong and Mumbai to Singapore, Introduced
e-ticketing on select routes, Introduced city check-in, advance airport check-in, Establishment of
call centres, Introduced SMS alerts in case of cancellations/delays will yield a positive result in
its profits and an increase in the passenger load factor in the ensuing years.
21. The Committee notes that profit of both the erstwhile Air India and Indian Airlines
has gone down substantially due to varied price of ATF, rapidly declining passenger
revenue yields on account of intense competition and deployment of excess capacity in the
market, etc. The Committee hopes that merger process of both these carriers will be
completed in time and this process will help the national carrier in long run in
consolidating its position in domestic and international market. The Committee hopes that
the synergisation process would help to improve the operational efficiency of both the
carriers. However, the Committee is of the view that NACIL should adopt an aggressive
marketing strategy to face the stiff competition at global level as well as domestic level
in order to have a level playing field with that of competitors. The Committee appreciates
the steps taken by NACIL to increase the market share of Air India with the fleet
strength of around 110. The Committee desires that the number of bilateral agreements
which were signed during the last year should be materialised to the maximum possible
extent. The Committee hopes that with the induction of new aircrafts in its fleet, Air
India can regain its glory and Maharaja status. The Committee desires that the NACIL
will soar to new heights by optimally utilizing its man power and available resources which
is not available with any of its competitor. The Committee hopes to see that NACIL will
come out of the blue and make profits in near future. The Committee recommends to the
Government that they may commission a study to know how the private airlines are
functioning including the financial freedom they are enjoying, their efficiency and
customer service. The findings of the study may be used for the improvement of NACIL.
The Committee may be apprised about the findings of such a study and the steps taken
to improve the performance of NACIL.

further recommends a proper valuation of the assets of the Nagpur airport including the

77. When the Committee asked about the demand and supply status of pilots and A TCs in the

carrier as well as induction of additional aircraft by private operators, the number of additional
aircraft in the next five years is estimated to reach a figure of 500, requiring an additional 5000
pilots at the rate of 5 sets of crew (2 pilots each) for every aircraft. In addition, another 1000
pilots would be required for private and non-scheduled operations over the next 5 years.

is 2051 and personnel in position is 1475 as on 1.3.2008. To a query on the recruitment of ATC
staff, the Ministry replied that at present, there are 1083 ATCOs and 392 JE (ATC) in position
including 39 trainees. Further, 323 posts had been created to meet the operational requirement
of Greenfield airports of Hyderabad and Bangalore. It is proposed to fill up these posts through
departmental promotion action as well as Direct Recruitment (DR) during the year 2008-09.
79. Recently, 300 posts of JE (ATC) and 68 posts of Manager (ATC) have been advertised.
Written tests for 300 posts of JE (ATC) are proposed to be conducted in May 2008. The
process is likely to be completed by the end of June 2008.
80. The Committee anxiously notes that the vacancy of 576 ATC is overburdening the
existing staff monitoring the herculeous task. Moreover, the Government has opened
Green Field Airports at Hyderabad and Bangalore. The Committee is surprised to note
that the Government has not taken any action in advance to start the recruitment
process to meet the operational requirement of these airports.
81. The Committee has been drawing the attention of the Government towards the
likely shortage of manpower for growing civil aviation sector. The Committee, however, is
constrained to observe that the Government has not been serious at all on this issue.
There is now shortage of trained manpower in every area of civil aviation sector. There
is a shortage of pilots and 576 posts of ATC out of sanctioned strength of 2051 are lying
vacant. The matter of setting up of flying training academy at Gondia, establishment of
training academy for BCAS, construction of BCAS headquarters building are still under
process. In the name of bringing in professionalisation in IGRUA, the training period
pilots have been reduced from two years to one year. Such situation could have been
avoided had the Government taken note of the recommendations of the Committee and
adopted the proactive approach in the matter.  The Committee hopes that in future

Aerodrome Inspectors which is a crucial for air safety. These inspectors inspect the
aircraft before flying and ensure that it is fit enough to perform its journey. The
Committee notes that the strength of aerodrome inspectors is much less than the

19
sanctioned strength. The Committee recommends that Government should take necessary
steps on priority to fill the vacancies as any shortage of trained man power to inspect the
aircraft before its flying will definitely compromise air safety playing with the lives of
passengers.
UNIFORM TAXATION OF ATF
84. The Committee finds that one of the major reasons for the poor financial performance
of the airline operators in the country is high cost of Aviation Turbine Fuel. Even though the
pricing of ATF is now on import parity basis, the rates applicable for domestic operations
continue to be significantly higher than that of international operations. The cost of A TF goes
up even further due to high rates of sales tax levied by the State Governments/Union Territory
Administration varying from 25 per cent to 30 per cent which affects the viability of domestic
airline operations.
85. The Committee while appreciating the steps taken by the State Governments
of Kerala and Andhra Pradesh in reducing the Sales Tax on ATF from 32 per cent to
4 per cent recommends that the Ministry pursue this long standing issue with other State
Governments so that uniformity of tax on ATF can be maintained. Since the Cost of fuel
is an important component of cost structure, reduction in taxes on ATF will definitely
have a positive impact on the airfares. The Committee once again recommends that
Ministry of Finance should sympathetically consider and give approval to the proposal of
Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding notifying ATF as ‘Declared Good’ under Section 14 of
Central Sales Tax Act on priority basis to all the aircrafts so that sales tax on ATF could
be contained within the maximum rate of 4 per cent. The Committee further recommends
that the Ministry of Finance may also discuss the issue with the State Governments and
try to persuade them to reduce the sales tax on ATF. The Committee is of the opinion
that the success of the concept of low cost carrier mainly depends on the taxation of ATF
which is very much on the higher side. The Committee feels that reduction in airfares
will bring more new passengers to the airports.

20
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ANNUAL PLAN 2007-08
The Committee notes that Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed to fully utilize the
outlay approved during 2007-08. This looks something strange at time when the civil
aviation sector is witnessing an unprecedented growth for past few years. The Ministry
anticipates to utilize an amount of Rs.11211.61 crore only out of the approved allocation
of Rs.12347.09 crore during the year 2007-08, which exemplifies the poor financial
management in the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The Committee feels that there is a lack
of proper planning in the various organisations of Ministry of Civil Aviation, as a result
of which the Ministry was unable to utilize optimally the approved outlays at its disposal.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Civil Aviation should impress
upon the concerned agencies to make a realistic assessment of their financial
requirements so that the allocations made do not remain unutilized. (Para 6)
BUDGET 2008-09 AND ANNUAL PLAN FOR 2008-09
The Committee feels that reduction in Budgetary support of the Ministry will
definitely have a negative impact on the expansion of aviation sector in North-Eastern
region as the approved budgetary support component does not include the outlay of
Rs.45.00 crores proposed to be given as a grant for the setting up of Greenfield Airport
at Pakyong, Sikkim. The Committee recommends that the Ministry may take this issue
with the Finance Ministry at RE stage and prevail upon them to grant more money to
ensure that works for project start well in time. The Committee expects that the
Government will ensure that the targets set for internal and extra budgetary resources
as well as external commercial borrowings from foreign banks/financial institutions for
bridging the gap in budgetary support will materialize. The Committee recommends that
the Ministry should take adequate steps during 2008-09 also to ensure optimum utilisation
of the enhanced allocations made to various organisations. (Para 11)
NATIONAL A VIATION COMPANY OF INDIA LIMITED
The Committee notes that profit of both the erstwhile Air India and Indian Airlines
has gone down substantially due to varied price of ATF, rapidly declining passenger
revenue yields on account of intense competition and deployment of excess capacity in the
market, etc. The Committee hopes that merger process of both these carriers will be
completed in time and this process will help the national carrier in long run in
consolidating its position in domestic and international market. The Committee hopes that
the synergisation process would help to improve the operational efficiency of both the
carriers. However, the Committee is of the view that NACIL should adopt an aggressive
marketing strategy to face the stiff competition at global level as well as domestic level
in order to have a level playing field with that of competitors. The Committee appreciates
the steps taken by NACIL to increase the market share of Air India with the fleet
strength of around 110. The Committee desires that the number of bilateral agreements
which were signed during the last year should be materialised to the maximum possible
extent. The Committee hopes that with the induction of new aircrafts in its fleet, Air
20

21
India can regain its glory and Maharaja status. The Committee desires that the NACIL
will soar to new heights by optimally utilizing its man power and available resources which
is not available with any of its competitor. The Committee hopes to see that NACIL will
come out of the red and make profits in near future. The Committee recommends to the
Government that they may commission a study to know how the private airlines are
functioning including the financial freedom they are enjoying, their efficiency and
customer service. The findings of the study may be used for the improvement of NACIL.
The Committee may be apprised about the findings of such a study and the steps taken
to improve the performance of NACIL. (Para 21)
AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA (AAI)
The Committee expresses its apprehension over the handing over of Nagpur airport
to JVC for a token sum of Re.1/-. The Committee is not convinced by the reasons given
by the Ministry for this whole episode. The Committee feels that this will set a wrong
precedent. After investing a large amount of public money for development and
modernization of this airport, the Committee sees no logic behind the decision of the
Government in handing over the airport to a JVC virtually free of cost. The Committee
further recommends a proper valuation of the assets of the Nagpur airport including the
land may be made and brought into the Books of the JVC so that the information is
available in the public domain. The Committee may be apprised of the further
developments in this front and a copy of MOU signed with the JVC may be sent to the
Committee for perusal. (Para 30)
The Committee feels that the enhanced annual outlay for Airports Authority of
India during this year will help the Authority to complete its ongoing projects in time and
match the aviation infrastructure at par with international standards and also with that
of boom in aviation sector. The Committee recommends that Airports Authority of India
should be given necessary financial freedom in selecting and executing the aviation
infrastructure projects with its potential and expertise in this field. The Committee hopes
that development of non-metro projects will be completed within the scheduled period as
these airports will help in easing the traffic congestion at metro airports. The Committee
feels that while the Airports Authority of India will develop, maintain and manage the air-
side upgradation and terminal modernization, the issue of city side development of these
airports should not become a hurdle in completing these airports. The Committee hopes
that in addition to these metro and non-metro airports, small cities having adequate
tourism potential should also be brought in the aviation map of the country and this could
be only possible by the active role of Airports Authority of India in developing unutilized
airstrips in such cities. The Committee desires that ongoing development works in the
North-Eastern sector should be given priority by the Airports Authority of India so that
necessary aviation infrastructure is developed in this region to give air connectivity to the
North-Eastern States. (Para 41)
PA WAN HANS HELICOPTERS LIMITED
The Committee is unhappy to note that the Board of Directors of Pawan Hans
Limited decided to stop the purchase of seven helicopters in 2007-08. The Committee
observes that this should not happen on the plea that in the coming year a large number
of helicopters have to be purchased and all of it can be purchased at one go. The
Committee recommends that the Pawan Hans should implement its activities in the
relevant year itself instead of postponing it year after year. (Para 48)

22
The Committee observes that the services of Pawan Hans are still underutilized.
The Committee feels that there is tremendous scope of utilizing the helicopter facility to
connect the remote tourist places. The Committee recommends that Pawan Hans
Helicopters Limited should prepare specific plans to diversify/connect to important tourist
places as a part of diversification of its operations. The Committee expects that the
approved outlay for new fleet acquisition will be fully utilized in the current financial
year. The Committee notes that entry of Pawan Hans in smaller aircraft operations will
definitely provide air connectivity in North-Eastern region and also to small cities of
tourist and commercial importance. The Committee desires to see that Pawan Hans uses
its resources to the maximum possible extent to make the Y ear of Helicopters a
successful one by expanding its horizon. (Para 52)
HOTEL CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED
The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the performance of Centaur Hotel,
Delhi which is not noteworthy. The Committee feels that the allocation of meager amount
of 6 crores will not improve its ambience which is very pathetic now. The Committee
recommends that measures should be taken by the Government to improve the
performance of the hotel with that of the other luxurious hotels in Delhi. (Para 55)
INDIRA GANDHI RASHTRIYA URAN AKADEMI
The Committee finds no merit in handing over the management of IGRUA to a
private organisation. The Committee feels that an institute receiving grants from the
Government and also having a good infrastructure which has been developed on public
money has been handed over to a private organisation with a simple excuse of
professionalisation of its management. This year also an amount of Rs. l.12 crores is
proposed to be provided by Government to IGRUA in the form grants-in-aid. The
Committee is of the opinion that simply professionalizing the management of an institute
will not give any positive output immediately. The Committee feels that the existing
management could have been given extra powers to improve the performance of this
akademi. The Committee expresses its displeasure on this issue and recommends that
remedial measures should be taken to ensure that the undertaking being managed by the
public money is not handed over to a private management on a platter. The Committee
also notes that after upgradation of infrastructure of IGRUA, the training period for pilots
will be reduced from two years to one year. The Committee hopes that this decision will
not affect the proficiency of pilots. (Para 62)
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF CIVIL A VIATION
The Committee hopes that DGCA will utilize its annual outlay to the fullest level
possible as it plays a vital role in regulating air traffic and air safety. The Committee is
constrained to note that though civil aviation sector is undergoing a boom in the country,
the Government is still in process of identifying the requirement of manpower of DGCA.
The Committee recommends that DGCA should address the issue of shortage of manpower
with all seriousness and recruitment of manpower should be started well in time so that
its core activities do not suffer further. There are media reports that Ministry is finding
difficulty to fill up the post of Director-General in DGCA. The Committee would like that
the post is filled up with the person having technical experience in the field of Civil
Aviation sector. (Para 66)

23
BUREAU OF CIVIL AVIATION SECURITY
The setting up of Headquarters building has been under consideration for quite a
long time. The Committee is constrained to note that the matter could not see the light
of the day till date for the one or other reason. Delay in construction of BCAS
Headquarters building has in turn affected the setting up of Training Academy of the
BCAS and restructuring and strengthening of the BCAS. Now the land issue has been
settled in respect of BCAS headquarters building at Delhi, the Committee hopes that the
proposal for restructuring and strengthening of BCAS and setting of Training Academy
will be finalized without delay. The Committee recommends to the Ministry that all out
efforts may be made to utilize the entire money for the purposes to which it is allocated.
(Para 69)
AERO CLUB OF INDIA
The country is in need of a large number of pilots. The Committee recommends
that the Government should adequately strengthen the Aero Club of India to produce and
train more pilots. (Para 70)
NATIONAL CIVIL A VIATION POLICY
The Committee is surprised to note that the much talked National Civil Aviation
Policy is not able to see light of the day even after considered discussions by committees
after committees. This shows a poor and lackadaisical approach of the Government in
announcing an important policy which is so much relevant at the time when aviation
sector is witnessing an unimaginable growth. The Committee feels that issues relating
level playing field for stakeholders, FDI in aviation sector and other air safety issues can
be well addressed by the New Civil Aviation Policy only. The Committee recommends that
the Government should come up with the National Civil Aviation Policy at the earliest as
a large number of private players entering the aviation sector in infrastructure side as
well as in air service side. (Para 72)
CHENNAI AND KOLKATA AIRPORTS
The Committee is constrained to note the matter of modernisation of Chennai and
Kolkata has been engaging the attention of the Government for considerably long time
but the matter is still under process. The Committee reiterates its earlier
recommendation that the modernisation of Chennai and Kolkata airports should be
completed on priority so as to ease the traffic over Delhi and Mumbai airports. The
Committee also desires that both these airports may be developed as international hubs
to cater to the needs of the people in the Eastern and Southern part of the country. The
Committee recommends that Airports Authority of IndIa should be given all the financial
and operational freedoms enjoyed by any private player in the field. The procedural
wrangles and red tapism should never be allowed to crop up in the functioning of Airports
Authority of India. The Committee opines that the modernization and development of
Chennai and Kolkata airports are a golden opportunity to prove the efficiency and mettle
of the Airports Authority of India and its employees. The Committee hopes that they will
stand up to the expectations reposed on them. The Committee hopes that the Airports
Authority of India will complete all the modernisation and developmental works of
Kolkata and Chennai airports within a specified time-frame. The Committee may be

24
apprised about the progress made by Airpor ts Authority of India in modernizing the
airports at Chennai and Kolkata. (Para 76)
SHORTAGE OF PILOTS AND ATCs
The Committee anxiously notes that the vacancy of 576 ATC is overburdening the
existing staff monitoring the herculeous task. Moreover, the Government has opened
Green Field Airports at Hyderabad and Bangalore. The Committee is surprised to note
that the Government has not taken any action in advance to start the recruitment
process to meet the operational requirement of these airports.
The Committee has been drawing the attention of the Government towards the
likely shortage of manpower for growing civil aviation sector. The Committee, however, is
constrained to observe that the Government has not been serious at all on this issue.
There is now shortage of trained manpower in every area of civil aviation sector. There
is a shortage of pilots and 576 posts of ATC out of sanctioned strength of 2051 are lying
vacant. The matter of setting up of flying training academy at Gondia, establishment of
training academy for BCAS, construction of BCAS headquarters building are still under

pilots have been reduced from two years to one year. Such situation could have been
avoided had the Government taken note of the recommendations of the Committee and
adopted the proactive approach in the matter. The Committee hopes that in future
Government will give necessary consideration to complete the projects in time in a time

The Committee hopes that provision of modern equipments at IGRUA and

pilots. The Committee recommends that necessary aid/grant should be given for starting
flying institutions so that the demand of pilots can be adequately taken care of. However,
availability of proper infrastructure for training of pilots and setting up of standards for
pilots training should also get proper consideration before giving licenses to new flying
institutes. The Committee hopes that initiatives taken by the Government will match the
demand and supply of pilots and ATCs in due course.
The Committee notes that the strength of aerodrome inspectors is much less than
the sanctioned strength. The Committee recommends that Government should take
necessary steps on priority to fill the vacancies as any shortage of trained man power to
inspect the aircraft before its flying will definitely compromise air safety playing with the
lives of passengers. (Para 80, 81, 82, 83)
UNIFORM TAXATION OF ATF

that the Ministry of Finance may also discuss the issue with the State Governments and
try to persuade them to reduce the sales tax on ATF. The Committee is of the opinion

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and
 Culture, having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and
 Thirty Ninth Report of the Committee on the Motor Vehicles Amendment Bill, 2007 *.
2.         The Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 15th May, 2007.  In pursuance of rules relating to the
 Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred** the Bill to the
 Committee on the 17 th May, 2007 for examination and report within three months. On the request being made by the
 Chairman of the Committee, Hon’ble Chairman had granted extension of time till the first day of last week of the
 Budget Session (second part) of the Parliament for the presentation of the report of the Committee on the aforesaid Bill.
3.          The Committee took oral evidence of the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Road Transport and
 Highways at its meeting held on the 18th July, 2007.
4.          The Committee heard the views of the representatives of .various stakeholders and individuals at its meeting
 held on the 4th October, 2007. 
5.         The Committee also considered the draft Report on the subject and adopted the same on  24th April,  2008.
6.          The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the Secretary and other officers of the Department of Road
 Transport and Highways and Ministry of Law and Justice for the assistance and inputs provided during deliberations on
 the provisions of the Bill. The Committee also acknowledges the contribution of representatives of various stakeholders
 and individuals who submitted their valuable suggestions on the provisions of the Bill.

Report
The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Bill, 2007 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 15 th May, 2007.  The
 Bill was referred to this Committee for examination and report.  Under the mandate, the Committee has examined the
 Bill and finalized the Report after ascertaining the views of various stakeholders and the nodal Department i.e.
 Department of Road Transport and Highways. 
2.         The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, a principal instrument for regulating motor vehicles was amended for the first
 time comprehensively in 1994.  Then some minor amendments were carried out in 2000 and 2001.  However, in recent
 past, Road Transport Sector had undergone many changes in terms of vehicle population, technological upgradation,
 increase in road accidents and vehicular pollution.  Many provisions of the Act had either lost its significance or started
 creating more hurdles rather than making the system smooth.  Moreover, there are a large number of provisions which
 are enforced by State Governments but they are dependant on Central Government for its approval.   There was also a
 clamour for restructuring Second Schedule which prescribes the structured compensation formula.
3.         Taking into account, all these aspects the Department endeavoured to bring out changes in the Act to make it
 suitable to the present day requirement.   The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Bill 2007 has undergone all stages of
 processes involved in the Amendment procedure i.e. consultation with all the stakeholders, vetting by Ministry of Law
 and approval of the Union Cabinet. 
4.         The Statement of object and reasons of the Bill states that Bill interalia, seeks to achieve the following:-
(i) to enhance penalties, wherever considered necessary, for violation of provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act,
 1988 with a view to ensure road safety and  discipline;
(ii) to provide for civil penalty in addition to the existing criminal liability. The amount realised by way of civil
 penalty shall be credited to the Solatium Fund which is to be used for the accident victims;
(iii) to confer more powers to States and Union territories, to make regional transport authorities more
 responsive in discharge of their duties and responsibilities;
(iv) to remove anomalies and rationalize provisions for emerging new needs and requirements ;
(v) to provide for a rationale and streamlining of provisions dealing with payment of appropriate compensation
 to road accident victims; and
(vi) to provide for settling of the claims directly by the insurer with a view to reduce the hardships of the
 accident victims and accelerate disposal of cases relating to compensation claims.
 5. The Department of Road Transport and Highways in their background note furnished to the Committee has brought
 out the reasons for the introduction of the Bill as follow:
5.1.Enhancement of penalties: 
The existing penalties do not have deterrent effect as in many cases the penalty is as low as Rs.100/-.  The issue
 of enhancement of penalties was also subject matter of High Court of Delhi in a PIL.  Hence the penalties for
 various offences are proposed to be enhanced to make it more deterrent.   The enhancement has been proposed

5.2.Delegation of Power to States: 
It was felt necessary to delegate powers to the States to recognize certificates issued by Institutions/Automobiles
 associations for grant of learner's licences for driving non-transport vehicles and also to make Automobile
 Associations eligible for recognition as testing bodies for driving licences for such vehicles.   Hence, powers are
 proposed to be delegated to States to exercise control on driving training schools to supervise construction of
 driving tracks and prescribe standards and fees to be charged. The State would be empowered, without waiting
 for the directions from the Central Government, to restrict the number of stage carriage or contract carriage
 permits in cities.  Such powers are needed to control traffic, reduce congestion and encourage public transport. 
 The State Governments are being empowered to frame rules for validation of special permits issued to
 stage/contract carriages for regions outside their area of operation to take care of special
 occasions/requirements.  Similarly, the States are proposed to be empowered to nationalize routes including
 portions of inter-State routes lying in their respective State, if the same is covered by inter-State Agreement.   At
 present, such cases require Central Government's prior approval. The State Governments are also proposed to be
 empowered to frame rules regarding installation of speed-governors and fog lights. The State Governments are
 being proposed to be authorized to appoint auditors to audit inspection and maintenance facilities for in use
 vehicles.
5.3.      Responsiveness of Transport authorities: 
5.3.1   A number of new provisions for amendments are aimed at removing difficulties citizens face in dealing
 with Regional/Transport Authorities.   Time limits are being proposed for disposal of appeals for non-
grant/cancellation of driving licences and non-issuance of registration certificates and permit.
5.3.2  For vehicles being operated under hire-purchase financing schemes, the registering authority would be
 required in terms of the proposed amendments to inform the financier, original registering authority and the last
 registering  authority by Registered Post with Acknowledgement due, in respect of many subsequent
 transactions.  A provision for refund of pro-rata unutilized one-time tax paid on non-transport vehicles which
 are transferred for registration in another State is being proposed.  It is also being proposed that the official
 checking any motor vehicle has to establish his identity and issue a standardized receipt if he wishes to seize the
 driving licence. The time limit to apply for transfer of insurance certificate upon purchase of a vehicle from
 another owner is being proposed to be increased from fourteen to thirty days.
5.4       New Requirements and Rationalization of anomalies and Enabling Provisions: 
5.4.1.   Various players in road transport industry are being brought under the Carriage by Road definition of "common
 carrier" under the Carriage by Road Act.  As there are linkages between the proposed "Carriage by Road Act" and the
 Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the definition of "common carrier" as contained in the former is being added to the latter. In
 view of the current emphasis on encouraging technologies for environment friendly vehicles, the definition of "battery
 operated vehicles" is being added to the Act. "Multi-axle vehicle" is being defined and "dealer" is being re-defined to
 remove the ambiguity in their application and interpretation in the field.
5.4.2.   It is being proposed that the applicant for driving licence for transport vehicles should have a driving licence of a
 light motor vehicle for two years, instead of one year as at present, before applying for the driving licence. Other
 changes proposed include substitution of "motor cycle below 50 cc" for "motor cycles without gear" in the rule relating
 to driving licence to reflect the change in technology relating to vehicles without gears. It is being proposed that the
 driving licence of any driver found driving under the influence of alcohol as evidenced by the prescribed tests to be
 suspended.
5.4.3.   The Central Government would have powers to make rules on design of bus and truck bodies to ensure safety
 and comfort of these vehicles. It has been proposed that consignor also to be held responsible besides driver or owner
 of the vehicle for the overloading as overloading is mostly done with the knowledge of consignor and has emerged as a
 major danger to the safety of road users and longevity of the road infrastructure.   The Motor Vehicle Departments
 officials would necessarily have to weigh the vehicles suspected to be overloaded, off-load the excess load, and not

5.5.Third Party Insurance and compensation to road accident victims: 
5.5.1.   Around 1.4 million cases relating to Motor Accident Claims have piled up in the Motor Accident Claim
 Tribunals (MACTs) and courts.  Instances have also come to notice where more than one claim has been filed under
 different sections of the Act. There is thus a need for a more rational and clear -cut structure for payment of
 compensation to road accident victims.   The proposal is to provide for two alternative options for the victims or their
 legal heirs to either go in for a simplified and attractive Structured Compensation Formula (based on age and income
 profile of the victim) on a "No Fault Principle" or for full liability of vehicle-owners/insurers by proving the fault or
 negligence of the vehicle/driver.  At present it is possible to do both giving rise to endless litigation.   This is causing
 delay in payment of compensation to the victims and adversely affecting the insurance companies who are therefore
 reluctant to provide such insurance policies.
5.5.2.   A number of provisions aiming at rationalization relating to payment of interest, filing of combined claims in
 case of multiple dependents, simplification and revision of the structured compensation formula, the solatium scheme
 for hit and run accidents and obligation of the insured vehicle owners to provide certain documents to the insurers are
 also part of the proposed Bill. An enabling provision is also being proposed to enable insurance companies with the
 consent of the claimant to settle the claims out of court and come to the MACT or civil court for ratification.   It is
 expected that the proposed provisions will reduce the number of cases pending before MACTs/Courts and benefit the
 victims.
5.5.3.   At present, there is no provision in the Act relating to civil liability of a driver if he causes accidents.   Hence, it
 is proposed to introduce civil liability of  a driver by providing penalty upto Rs.5000/- if one drives a motor vehicle in
 rash or negligent manner, causing injury to a person or damages to any property.  The amount so realized shall be
 credited to the Solatium Fund and shall be utilized for payment of compensation to the road accident victims.

37.       One of the stakeholders in their memorandum submitted to the Committee has stated that through various
 proposals the financiers of Motor Vehicles have been given enormous powers. In the 1994 amendment the financiers
 had been given too much authority which taken together with the present amendment bill almost makes them the
 dictators and now they possess the authority to choke some of the freedoms provided to the citizens in the constitution
 of India.
38.       The financiers lobby now have say in all kinds of transactions that take place in the RTO offices.  Every owner
 is required to take no objection certificates from the financiers almost every time they need to make an application to
 the motor vehicle administration.   A few examples are renewal of permit, issue of all duplicates in cases of loss,
 alteration of vehicle that does not affect the type of vehicle in any way, etc.   These do not affect their interests in any
 way.  Further, all the customers are forced to sign "n" number of documents at the time of grant of loan like, blank
 termination of loan forms, blank transfer of ownership forms, etc.  These help them in seizing the vehicles illegally, by
 force, even in cases where the repayment histories of the customers are exemplary, and then they use these blank forms
 to dispose of the vehicles to another client.
39.       In view of the above, the Committee feels that the Motor Vehicle Act may be amended in such a way that does
 justice to both the financiers and the customers.  The amendment should also give option to the motor vehicle
 administration to overrides the requirement of the no objection certificate after giving both sides a chance to present his
 case. The Govt. should also come forward with concrete proposals to stop the financiers from adopting the bullying
 tactics to recover the vehicle loans. 
40.       One of the stakeholders submitted to the Committee an example of the safety measures recommended by
 PACTS   (Parliamentary Advisory Council for Transport Safety of the United Kingdom).  According to PACTS road
 traffic law contributes to reducing casualties by providing a framework for safe road use and laying down clear
 standards for driver and road behaviour.  Its existence also details drivers and roads from breaching those standards.  To

 be effective as a way of preventing deaths and injuries the law must be reasonable and appropriate and it must be
 communicated to and understood by all road users.  The Committee feels that the Road Traffic Law should, therefore,
 define acceptable standards and behaviours on the road and in doing so should provide guidance for road users.  The
 Committee recommends that the Government should endeavor to implement the spirit of the suggestions made by
 PACTS in its report on Road Traffic Law and Enforcement. 
41.       Another aspect brought before the Committee by one of the stakeholders is the insufficiency of the road
 signage.  They have stated that the road sign has been updated by the Indian Road Congress in 2001 but the First
 Schedule to the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 has not been amended to incorporate the changes.  This has left a major
 vacuum in road user education, the driver training as well as installation of signage as per law.  The Committee feels
 that if the signages in the schedule are obsolete or not keeping with the pace of the changing times, naturally there will
 remain a serious handicap in driver training and education.   The Committee also notes that there is no mention of road
 marking or traffic signals in the first schedule.  The Committee feels that this is a major shortcoming and recommends
 that the first schedule should be amended with comprehensive signs and symbols, road markings and signals as per the
 recommendations of the Indian Roads Congress.
42.       One of the stakeholders brought to the notice of the Committee that the maximum, permissible load for different
 goods vehicles vis-à-vis overloading of vehicles is another issue that needs review.  The maximum Gross Vehicle
 Weight of a two axle truck has been fixed at 16200 kgs.  As a result the maximum load that can be legally carried in
 such a vehicle is found to be not in excess of 10 tonnes.  Now, with the advent of new and better technology in the
 automobile sector, the vehicles manufactured at present are often found to be efficient enough to carry much more than
 the actual permissible load.  This has allowed the owners a scope for overloading of their vehicles to a certain extent as
 this does not necessarily harm their vehicles.   State Governments also loose revenue in the form of state taxes as in
 most states the tax is dependant on the ULW/GVW of the vehicle.   Further, as the GVW, that is actually to be arrived,
 depends on the tyres fitted in the vehicle (as per tyres rules in the C M V Rules, 89), there are scopes for fitment of
 bigger tyres which in turn will mean higher ULW/GVW and therefore, higher permissible load.  The matter needs to be
 reviewed jointly by the Government, manufacturers, CIRT and ARAI, as this will mean higher government revenues
 too. The Committee recommends that a high level committee needs to be formed to explore the possibilities and put
 forward their suggestions in this respect.

            Another aspect brought before the Committee by one of the stakeholders is the insufficiency of the road
 signage.  They have stated that the road sign has been updated by the Indian Road Congress in 2001 but the
 First Schedule to the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 has not been amended to incorporate the changes.  This has left a
 major vacuum in road user education, the driver training as well as installation of signage as per law.  The
 Committee feels that if the signages in the schedule are obsolete or not keeping with the pace of the changing
 times, naturally there will remain a serious handicap in driver training and education.  The Committee also
 notes that there is no mention of road marking or traffic signals in the first schedule.  The Committee feels that
 this is a major shortcoming and recommends that the first schedule should be amended with comprehensive
 signs and symbols, road markings and signals as per the recommendations of the Indian Roads Congress.

REPORT 
National Highways (NH) are the main arteries running through the length and breadth <>f 
the country. They play vital role in the economic and ~oc i al upliftmcnt of the country . Today 
when economic growth and prosperity are the hall mark of the modern age. N;ttion;d 
Highways assume still more important role in the atmosphere of humming business and 
commercial activity. Tite proper upkeep and maintenance of national highways is, therefore 
our prime concern. National Highways have witnessed vast expansion in rec;ent years and 
brought even the most distant places in the country into the economic mainstream. Nation .. ! 
Highways extend to 34058 Kms. approximately connecting the State capitals, major ports , 
industrial complexes , tou rist destinations, serving de(cnce needs and providing links to 
adjacent countries. These form the pri mary 11etwork to carry long and medium . distance 
goods and passenger m•ffic. 
2. National Highways is a Centra l subject in terms of "Entry 23" of the Union List under 
the Seventh Schedule . The entire expenditure on the development, construction . 
improvement and maintenance of national highways is met by the Governmem of India. The 
national highway Act, 1956 ( 48 of 1956) governs the matters related to the Nat ional 
Highway System. The works are, however. executed by the respectiv e State Governments 
and Border Road Development Board (B.R .D.B ,) in respect of certain highways on 
"agency" basis through Annual Plan/Five Year Plans. The Governmcm constit utt:d National 
Highway Authority of india (NHAI) in June 1989 in order to develop, maintain and manage 
the national highways and other highways vested in or entrusted to it by the Government. 
Initially the Authority was expected to execute the externally aided projects such as those of 
ADB and World Bank and later to take over the ent ire charge of development and 
maimenance of national highways which has bee n done so far by the State Governments on 
agency basis. The Author ity however is yet to become operational. The Secretary. Ministry 
of Surface Transport while deliberating before the Committee on 28.10 .94 stated that the 
I 
Authority could not become operational as the government could not find adequate 
personne l for it. He also informed the Committee that the Authority would get fully 
operationalised in a few months. 
3. The Commillee is not convinced with the reasons put forth by the Ministry of Surface 
Transport for non-operation of N.R.A.l. as five years have elapsed since its inception. The 
Committee feels that this issue was taken up in a lackadaisical manner. It appears that 
Government was not serious to operationa lise the N.H.A.I. The Commillee deplores such 
altitude of the Government and impresses upon il now to make serious efforts to see that the 
Authority becomes operlllional at the earliest to fulfil its objectives. 
Major coiiStraints and SJrategy in the 8th Plan 
4. 'fhe Plan document (1992-97) states that over the years, the National Highway System 
has come under severe strain due to high rate of growth in traffic volume. Selection and 
priontisation of different s.egmems of road network for improvement and upgradation 3JC 
handicapped by the absence of reliable data. There i$ no systematic collection of data on 
road traffic because of the absence of traffic recording and reporting procedures, multipilicty 
of transport ••gcncic> ~nd preponderance of single vehicle operators. Attempts had been 
lllilde in the pa>t by different groups rtnd Committees to build up estunates of wad traffic for 
goods and passengers by different methods and under different assumptions. These traffic 
estimates and projections showed considerab le variations. It is, therefore, necessary to 
undertake periodic traffic surveys to update the information at the regular intervals.

5. Road traffic is bound to increase substantially in the next ten yean. The major 
deficiencies/constraints hindering the development of National Highways are inadequate 
road pavements, breadth and thickness and presence of old, weak and narrow bridges and 
culverts. The maintenance of NH System is further hindered by lack of adequate funds. 
Funds generally do not exceed 60% of normal requirement of the national highways. 
6. The existi ng deficiencies in national highways would require construct ion of missing 
links, four-laning and two-laning of various sections, construction of bridges nnd bypusscs 
etc. According to the Eighth Plan document, the tint priority would be given tl1 comp lete 
the ongoing works. For systematic development of the NH system, different strategies 
would need to be adopted for low, medium and high volume traffic dcn~ity routes. 
Capacity augmentation of high density corridors carrying more than 15,000 Passenger Car 
Unit~ (PCU) traffic per day through four-laning will need to be taken up during the Eighth 
Plan For selected high density comdors, it may be necessary to consider expressway 
facility for rapid and safe movement of fast traffic. Levy of tolls may be con,idcred for 
highway users . For national highways carrying medium traffic density. traffic upto 15,000 
PCUs , strengthening of pavement and widening to two-lanes including rccon,truction of 
bridges, wherever necessary, need to be taken up. For low traffic density route~ carrying 
traffic upto 5.000 PCU, widening to two lanes may be considered only on a selective basis, 
depending upon the resource availability. However, weak and narrow bridges have to be 
replaced. 
7. As regards additions to the National Highway system, it would be necessary to adopt 
a very selective approach in view of the resource constrai nts and the need to give priority 
to removal of deficiencies on the existing NH system.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf
this One Hundred Fortieth Report on ‘Promotion of Tourism in Jammu and Kashmir’.
2. India has always been an attractive tourist destination from far and wide since ages.
Paradoxically, however, India has not been able to exploit this potential. The Committee, therefore,
was of the opinion that much remains to be done to exploit tourism potential significantly, and India
has a long way to go in this regard, it is with this background that the Committee decided to
undertake the promotion of tourism in India as a special study. To begin with, the Committee
decided to take up the State of Jammu and Kashmir first, followed by the North-Eastern Region
for this purpose. Accordingly, the Committee undertook a study visit to Jammu and Kashmir from
the 1st-6th June, 2008. During the visit, the Committee selected four major areas that were of vital
importance to the promotion of tourism at any place. The selected areas were: schemes/efforts
made for developing tourism sector per se ; development and maintenances of national highways in
the State; increasing air connectivity and expansion/modernization of airports and; protection and
preservation of ancient monuments that are aplenty in the State.
3. The Committee found that the Jammu and Kashmir despite having all the features of a
tourist heaven, its potential remains largely unutilized. The near absence of adequate tourist
infrastructure, the Committee feels is main reason behind this. The Committee was apprised of the
difficulties that came in the way of promotion of tourism in the State such as restriction of entry
of tourist, poor infrastructure, lack of transport facility, poor security and road-air network etc.
The Committee, therefore, decided to present a report focusing mainly on these aspects.
4. The Committee expresses its gratitude to the officers of the Ministry of Tourism, Ministry
of Culture, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Ministry of Civil Aviation, Airport Authority
of India, National Aviation Company of India Limited, National Highways Authority of India,
Archaeological Survey of India and Officers of the Department of Tourism and Culture of
Government of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council, Tour-Travel
and Hotelier Association of Jammu and Kashmir, House Boat Owners Association and others for
their cooperation in furnishing the required feedback and information in connection with the
examination of the subject and also for making valuable suggestions for improving the tourism
scenario in the State.
5. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 11th August, 2008.

REPORT
Tourism being one of the world’s fastest growing industries today enjoys a vital
significance in the overall development of a country, mainly due to its multiplier effect-on
different walks of life. India too is not an exception in this regard; Tourism is the second largest
export industry in India. Foreign tourist arrival here rose from 3.46 million in 2004 to 5 million
in 2007. Tourism made a significant contribution to India’s foreign exchange earnings, which
grew from $ 6.17 billion (Rs.27,944 crore) in 2004 to $ 11.96 billion (Rs.49,413 crore) in
2007. The share of India in world tourism receipts went up from 0.65 per cent in 2002 to 1.21
per cent in 2006. The contribution of tourism to GDP of the country had been 6.11% in 2004,
while employment in tourism sector both direct and indirect had been 41.8 million in 2003,
which accounts for 8.74% of total employment in the country.
2. Such an impressive growth in tourism notwithstanding, India’s share in the world’s
tourist traffic was a mere 0.55 per cent in 2007. While the number of tourists visiting
India and earnings therefrom may be increasing, its slow growth rate as well as
insignificant share in world’s tourism has always been a cause of concern to this
Committee.
3. India has always been an attractive tourist destination from far and wide since ages. It
being a land of the most ancient civilization, long and chequered history, birth place of many
religion and sects; its varied topography and climatic conditions, serene and beautiful Himalayas,
long sea-coast, deserts, forests with contrasting flora and fauna, make India to have immense
tourist potential. Paradoxically, however, India has not been able to exploit this potential.
The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that much more needs to be done to exploit
our tourism potential significantly, if not fully, and we have a long way to go in this
regard. It is with this thinking that the Committee decided to undertake the promotion of
tourism in India as a special study. To begin with, the Committee decided to take up the State
of Jammu and Kashmir first followed by the North-Eastern Region for this purpose.
4. Jammu and Kashmir is one of the most attractive tourist destinations, both for foreign
as well as domestic tourists, which include Jammu, Kashmir valley and Ladakh region. Kashmir
valley is perched securely between bewitching snow-clad peaks, glaciers, interspersed with
beautiful lakes and famous gardens. The emerald blue skies peeping through the chinks of the
clouds, the tall chinar trees swaying to the rhythm of the gusts of wind make the surrounding
breath-taking. It is, therefore, rightly described as the ‘paradise on the earth’. Existence of
important shrines, oldest monasteries, temples and cave temples in all the three regions is other
attraction for the tourist. Jammu is considered to be a hub of pilgrim tourism in the State being
abode of Mata V aishno Devi attracting millions of tourists/pilgrims throughout the year. The valley
has immense potential for adventure tourism such a mountaineering, trekking, skiing, rafting,
hand-gliding and para sailing besides leisure tourism. The cold arid desert area of Ladakh
comprises two districts namely, Leh and Kargil and its surreal landscape has often been termed
as ‘moonland’.
DEVELOPMENT OF TOURISM IN JAMMU AND KASHMIR
5. Till 1989, tourism had been the major economic activity of the State. During the
past one decade, however, the tourist arrival received a major set back affecting the
economic activity of the State adversely due to difficult circumstances prevailing in the
State. But, the things appears to have been improving slowly particularly during the last
a few years. Development of tourism in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, the Committee

2
notes has received priority both by the Central Government as well as the State
Government.
6. The Committee during its visit to Srinagar and Leh discussed the subject “Development
of tourism in Jammu and Kashmir” with the representatives of Union Ministry of Tourism,
Government of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council. It also
spoke to the Hotel and Restaurants Federation, Houseboats Owners Association, J and K Shikara
Union, Tourism Hotel Alliance, Travel Agents Society of Kashmir, Travel Agents Association of
India, J and K, Tours Operators Association and Tourist Taxi Operators Union etc. with a view
to ascertaining their views/suggestions on different issues.
7. The State Department of Tourism submitted before the Committee that the State had
taken different initiatives, but much remains to be done to exploit the tourism potential to the
maximum extent. Tourism had been an important and major contributor to the State’s economy.
Keeping this in view, the Government of Jammu and Kashmir had declared tourism as an
industry, extending a number of concessions and incentives. The emphasis has been to revive the
traditional tourist circuits including tourism marketing by involving local travel trade in direct
marketing through the State Tourism Department. The following strategies and initiatives have
been chalked out by the State Department of Tourism to promote Brand Kashmir and to woo
tourists from the domestic and international markets:
➢ Focus on Marketing–Hon’ble Chief Minister, Jammu and Kashmir is personally leading
the campaign, in the country and abroad;
➢ Delinking of Tourism from Law and Order Situation;
➢ Tourism projected as a normal economic activity;
➢ Home and National Media impressed not to hype tourist arrivals;
➢ Increased participation in international Tourism marts; Revitalization of Brand Kashmir;
➢ Focus on expanding the domestic market-promotional campaigns in non-metros like
Indore, Baroda, Nagpur, Pune;
➢ Involvement of private tourism players in marts and festivals;
➢ Publicity in all media;
➢ Publicity grants increased for 2008-09;
➢ Identification and opening up of new areas;
➢ 19 high powered development authorities created for integrated and focused
development of identified areas in all three regions of the State;
➢ Gulmarg, Pahalgam, Sonamarg, Yousmarg, Dodapathri, Verinag, Kokernag, Leh, Kargil,
Patnitop, Lakhanpur-Sarthal, Aharbal, Wular-Manasbal, Zanskar, Rajouri, Poonch,
Bhaderwah, Kishtwar, Surinsar-Mansar;
➢ Master Plans being prepared for land use;
➢ Environment concerns will be addressed;
➢ Involvement of locals in hospitality sector;
➢ Many areas are also being developed outside the jurisdiction of development
authorities—Gurez, Bangus, Baramulla, Uri, Botapathri;

3
8. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the State Government of Jammu
and Kashmir for development of Tourism in the State. However, the Committee feels that
the strategy and initiatives taken by the State require a more focused approach for
effective and structured growth. The Committee was informed that there was no ‘Tourism
Policy” for the State. The Committee is of the opinion that the policy supports would
certainly help achieves goals and targets in this sector more effectively. The Committee,
therefore, emphasizes the need to have a tourism policy in place. It also emphasizes that
the strategy for marketing tourism products of the State needs to be revisited for tapping
the domestic and International tourism markets. The State should endeavour to assess the
market trend and focus on diverse and varied tourism products of Jammu and Kashmir
targeting specially the domestic middle class tourists.
TOURIST ARRIVALS
9. Till 1989, tourism activities in the State were concentrated around Kashmir Valley, with
few visiting Ladakh and yet fewer interested in Jammu. But due to terrorist activities within the
Kashmir valley since 1989, tourist inflow received a major setback. This has affected the
economic stability as well as employment opportunities of its population. The Government of
Jammu and Kashmir explored the possibilities of its tourism revival and concentrated on Ladakh.
Further, religious traffic to Jammu went up from a few thousands to above 7 million in 2007.
The following table presents a clear picture of tourist arrivals in J and K since 1988 to 2007
and the projections for the year 2008. The 1988 was the peak year for the tourist arrivals in

witnessed an upswing. The arrival figures in the State are very encouraging and the tourists
graph is constantly rising since 2006. Further, the projections for tourist arrivals in the State
for 2008 are also very encouraging. It is expected that the valley will receive around 7 lakhs
tourists during the year besides more than 8 million pilgrims are expected to visit the region.
